subsubtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN ANNOUNCING POLICY CHANGES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, involving transportation. On April 6 of this year, the Minister of Transport appeared before the relevant standing committee and promised a new Air Canada Act, a new transportation act, a new ports policy and a re-examination of the St. Lawrence seaway. A year before that, the former minister of transport announced there would be a regional third level air policy and on March 14, 1972 his predecessor promised sweeping transportation changes involving the CNR, Air Canada and the Railway Act amendments. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That because of the unprecedented delay in implementing these various obvious and important changes, the present Minister of Transport make a statement on motions at the first opportunity explaining to the House the reasons for this procrastination and giving the precise date when Air Canada officials who have not appeared before the relevant committee of this House during the past three years-at that time the 1972 annual report of Air Canada was discussed-will appear.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REDUCTION IN BEEF IMPORTS FROM AUSTRALIA-EFFECT OF CHANGE IN METHOD OF ISSUING IMPORT PERMIT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question was to be directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, but in his absence I will direct my question to the former minister. It deals with the status of the Canadian beef industry.
In view of the obvious reluctance or, indeed, failure or refusal of the Minister of Agriculture to implement a tempo-, rary embargo on Australian and New Zealand beef and veal imports-but rather, the government has opted for import permit controls-will the minister assure the House, and particularly the Canadian beef industry, that beef imports from those sources will cease or at least be reduced substantially? This is a very important question because comparing boatload-ings from September to September from that source to Canada they appear to be up some 61 per cent. Can the minister comment on that situation?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REDUCTION IN BEEF IMPORTS FROM AUSTRALIA-EFFECT OF CHANGE IN METHOD OF ISSUING IMPORT PERMIT

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is obvious from the answer that the minister has been in cabinet for some time. I should like to shift now to the Prime Minister. The Address-Mr. Milne
ed even further. I am raising a question which surely many people are worried about, that is: Where has all our understanding on this question gone? Canada has been known all over the world ever since its beginning for its tolerance and for the way in which various groups in Canada have been able to get along together. I am alarmed, as I am sure is every member of the House and surely all responsible Canadians, at the harsh attitude being adopted by so many people at this time.
There are two or three points which I should like to raise at this time. I really do not understand-and I would like to be enlightened on this-why everyone seems to feel that it is only the federal government which has the responsibility for maintaining national unity and, in particular, why the Prime Minister should be the only person in Canada concerned about national unity and having responsibility for doing something about it. Surely, this is an issue that is the concern of everyone elected to the House, to the provincial legislatures or to municipal school boards-indeed, the concern of every Canadian.
I want to support very strongly the statement in the Speech from the Throne that institutional bilingualism will be continued with some sensitivity to its administration, that problems connected with it will be considered and that perhaps a different approach will be taken to the administration of the program. I think it is a natural progression of the original policy for us to speak at this time to provincial governments, provincial premiers and provincial ministers of education about introducing this program to the educational systems over which the provinces have jurisdiction. Judging from a widespread expression of opinion on this matter by many people, I believe it is generally agreed that this is how this problem should be handled. I hope people are not saying that this matter should be put off for another period of time so that we will not have to deal with it. I hope that all parents, school boards and departments of education see this clearly as a major responsibility and take it seriously, and that this policy will be implemented as quickly and effectively as possible. I really believe there will be two important results from this. First of all, graduates of the school systems will have a much better knowledge of both official languages than is the case at present, and, what is even more important, they will have a better understanding and a greater tolerance of their fellow Canadians than they do now.
I think that this country cannot stand much more of the type of conflict that has been experienced in the past year or so. Really, the Anglophones and Francophones will have to approach this issue with a fundamentally different attitude and a much better understanding of each other's position on this. One of the real problems is the acceptance of change, an understanding of the dynamics of change and how it comes about. An example of this lack of understanding was the recent air traffic controllers' controversy in which extremists on both sides did nothing to solve the problem but in fact made it worse. This matter has been referred to many times in detail. This time I want to touch on it briefly. I could not understand
[Mr. Milne.)
the position of the Anglophones who are opposed to even having a feasibility study done in this matter, no more than I could understand the most vocal people on the other side who thought this should be a question of policy without any prior study being carried out of the feasibility of such a policy or any prior undertaking to explain to the rest of Canada why it is so important.
In raising this issue I wish to say that I represent many Air Canada employees and I believe that the best way of solving this issue is to undertake a study to look at the whole matter from a logical point of view, airport by airport, and to examine such matters as density and mix of traffic, sophistication of control tower equipment, as well as many other such issues, and based on this study to come up with a policy decision.
During the last summer I spoke to many of my constituents on the matter of bilingualism and I am concerned about how poorly the Official Languages Act is understood. Many people raised this issue in the context of "shoving French down my throat", but when the policy was explained to the same people they agreed that it was entirely reasonable. It seems to me that one of the fundamental things that the government, that we as supporters of the government, and that all members of the House should do, because this policy was supported by each and every party, is to go out in the country and reassure the people regarding the Official Languages Act and explain it to them. I believe that once it is explained to them, acceptance of it will be widespread. I believe that the problem at present is the misconception of the policy. Surely, we have the responsibility to explain the Act and the policy.
I would be pleased if the government would also take a look at the implementation of the bilingualism program in the Crown corporations. I have been told that there is not much opportunity for language training in either of the official languages for employees of Crown corporations who wish to learn the other language to advance their careers. One of the concerns they have relates to the method of selecting people. People who do not have the capability in a second language have no opportunity to gain a standing in the other language. That is a situation which bears consideration, and I hope that in terms of the administration of the Official Languages Act the government will do so.
Any partnership, whether it is a business relationship or whatever, is really based on three things. It is based on understanding of the other person's point of view; it most certainly has to be based on an adjustment to that other person's point of view; and most important, it must be based on a very high level of communication. If anything should happen in Canada, there should be a greatly increased understanding of the hopes, aspirations and rights of other people, some adjustment in everyone's point of view to accommodate those things and certainly a good deal of communication between various language groups to make sure that the concerns of both sides are well understood.

During the summer the Olympic Games took place and the Queen was here to open them. During her stay she spoke at a banquet, and I thought that she stated the situation with regard to the language problem better than I had heard it stated before. I should like to review three simple statements she made which I thought were very important, and I quote from her remarks of July 24 as follows:
There can be mutual enrichment only if each group has a secure and vital cultural life of its own to share with the other. It is important, therefore, for both French speaking and English speaking Canadians to maintain the integrity of their own language and culture.
How Canada resolves her political and constitutional differences is her own affair, but how she resolves her linguistic and cultural problems matters to thoughtful people everywhere.
The world, all too familiar with the tragic price of conflict between peoples of different race, language, religion and culture, can look to Canada for a better example and for a renewal of the human spirit. It can look to her for a practical demonstration of how two strong communities can live together in peace, drawing from each other's strengths, respecting each other's differences.
That is why your words, Prime Minister, about the growing mutual awareness, curiosity and respect among French speaking and English speaking Canadians, bear a message of great hope for both Canada and the world at large.
Her Majesty's remarks were well received by all Canadians who heard them, and those who did not have the opportunity to hear them should review her remarks because what she was saying was that resolving this problem is one of the fundamental things which has to be done if we are to survive as a strong and united country.
I would like to comment briefly on one particular aspect of the economy, but first I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). I think Canada is fortunate to have a minister of his capability. He is one of the more courageous Canadians, one of the fairest and one of the most consistent. All the way through this difficult period in the economy he has demonstrated the type of leadership which is important to Canada and which will correct some of the economic problems we have. His actions have not always been the most popular, and he has not always taken the easiest stances, but 1 think they have been the correct ones.
I have been a strong supporter of the guidelines. However, I have one concern. I hope that if there is to be further revision of the program, it will be in the area of rewarding productivity or highlighting it as one of the major forces in the economy.
Many people have spoken and have used many facts and figures to support their view of the situation we face with regard to exports as well as the ability to compete inside Canada with people exporting to Canada. We have some real problems, and many of them could be solved by attaching more importance to productivity. The word "productivity" does not seem to have captured the interest or attention of organized labour or management. As I listen to various groups talk about it, management seems to be saying only that we should have a lower wage scale in Canada, and labour seems to be saying that it should have a larger share of the national economy. It seems to me that the aims of both could be realized by seriously striving for greater productivity. That is what is needed for us to remain strong in the years ahead in
The Address-Mr. Milne
terms of having a viable manufacturing sector, particularly that part of it which is related to our export market.
The Speech from the Throne announced an intention to set up a collective bargaining information centre. I hope it will deal not just with compensation, the relationship of various groups and the broad economic conditions under which we operate but that it will also address itself sincerely to the question of productivity. Surely, emphasizing productivity in Canada at the present time is very important, and such things as workers' councils should be taken seriously because many people working in plants have some very good ideas as to how productivity could be improved.
There is another aspect which is equally important. No matter where we go we hear the statement that no one wants to work anymore. Quite often the people who are making that statement are having expense account lunches or drinks. If that statement is true, it is certainly true on the side of management as well as on the side of labour. This country needs to go back to a very aggressive marketing stance and a very aggressive industrial design position. We have had a few years of extraordinarily good times, and both labour and management have benefitted tremendously. Now, we have to realize that times are not as easy, and we have to go back to some of the fundamentals which enable companies to achieve success; that is, through high productivity, through good industrial design and through extremely strenuous efforts in marketing. This is particularly true in Canada where we depend so much on export markets for the well-being of our economy.
Compared with countries such as Japan, France, and strangely enough, Britain, our productivity is lagging. I understand that our productivity increase last year was in the order of 2 per cent compared with 6 per cent in Japan, 5 per cent in France and 3 per cent in Britain. We really must do something about that. I do not quite know why the measuring of productivity, which has been encouraged and used for many years in many European countries, has not really caught on in North America, and particularly in Canada. I suppose it has been a factor in the auto industry for a few years, but apart from that, it has not been a major consideration in collective bargaining. I hope in the future that both management and labour will see some of the perils which are down the road, because of the high return for labour and the lack of a superlative effort in marketing. I hope they will see where that will lead us. We should pause and look at productivity and effective bargaining. Perhaps the benefits of increased productivity could be shared between employees and employer and not, as in the past, go only to the employer.
I should like to make a few comments on agriculture, Mr. Speaker. I have said a number of times in this House that one of the fundamental objectives of this government should be that we be essentially self-sufficient in food. It may seem strange that I raise this issue at a time when we have a surplus of milk powder and are not short of beef cattle or other commodities, but there are one or two things that I should like

October 18, 1976
The Address-Mr. Milne
to raise in a general way. The minister might like to give some thought to them.
I am concerned about our future inventory of farmers, Mr. Speaker. I understand that the average age of our farmers is over 55 years. There has been a tremendous increase in productivity in the last five or six years as the old concept of small family farms gave way to larger family farms which use larger equipment than has ever been used in eastern Canada. Fewer farmers are doing more farming, but how long can that be sustained unless young people become farmers? Through provisions of the capital gains tax this government was able to be of tremendous assistance to farmers in that they could keep a farm in production without attracting capital gains tax after the death of the owner.

speechtext: Who introduced capital gains tax in the first instance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is a fair taxation measure and I should like to discuss its application to incorporated farms.
Through extension programs many provincial governments counselled farmers to incorporate and now, having done so, they find themselves on the wrong side of the proposition when it comes to capital gains tax at the time of the death of the owner. The difficulty is that most incorporated farms have associated with them some type of processing facility or trucking business, for example; generally speaking, such an operation is more than just an ordinary farm. I would argue the case that the land portion of an incorporated farm should have the same provision in the Income Tax Act applied to it as a non-incorporated farm when it comes to the capital gains tax.
I do not argue that the associated business of the farm should escape capital gains tax; if that were so it would be logical for the small business to ask for the same extension.
I think if our national objective is to have an inventory of farmers and to keep ourselves self-sufficient in food, we should consider exempting the land portion of the incorporated farm from capital gains tax. The value of land, particularly in Ontario and I suppose the same situation exists around large metropolitan areas in other provinces, has always been high. It used to be, however, that while land on the periphery of metropolitan and urban areas was very costly, about 150 miles or 200 miles away land was substantially cheaper. A farmer could sell property near a large urban area and re-establish himself or his family in agriculture some distance away. That has changed and land some distance from urban areas has increased in price.
I think this is another case which should cause us to look again at the capital gains tax and consider whether money realized from the sale of land, which is reinvested in land for agricultural purposes at some other location but for the same farm family, could not also escape this tax. Sometimes when a farmer sells land near an urban area on which he may have a long term mortgage, by the time he has purchased another farm and has renovated it so that it is comparable to with the one he sold, he ends up with a substantial debt. Many farm
[Mr. Milne.)
families decide it is just not worth while and, as a result, the children do not stay in farming. I am not sure we can afford this loss, Mr. Speaker.
There are two other aspects of agriculture that I should like to mention at this time. The first is marketing boards. I am sure there are not many members in this House who support organized marketing more strongly than I do. I spent a number of years in rural extension work and I saw many poultry farmers go from boom to bust, back and forth. I saw many farmers lose their farms to feed companies because of the real relationship of what was being produced to what the market could bear. I strongly supported the concept of marketing boards because I thought at that time, as I am sure most people did, that it was right and proper that they should be producer boards. But in some areas, I think we should look carefully at the marketing board concept and make sure the board is representative of the entire industry.
The proposed national chicken marketing agency for broiler chickens would protect the producer as well as the integrated supplier in terms of feed, hatchery and processing. A loss in one segment could be offset by profits in other segments, but I would argue the case for the independent processor who seems to be left out of the plan. At the present time it seems he is the only one who is taking any real risk and he has no protection whatsoever. I can see the danger that he might disappear from chicken broiler farming, and I should like to be on record as being in favour of processors as well as producers having a role in the marketing concept.
During question period today the inquiries were predominantly related to the beef industry and meat coming into this country. There are two distinct trends evident in our society today. When you drive around the cities, the growth of the fast food outlet, and the tremendous increase in the number of steak houses is evident. I do not know why our beef industry does not gear itself to produce more for this market. I have been told that most of these steak houses want imported beef because of consistent quality and taste, and that the fast food outlets want it because we do not produce enough of the type used. Surely, the Canadian Cattlemen's Association could analyse the market trends and supply the type of meat preferred. Rather than the beef industry continuing to produce cattle of the type it has in the past while the consumer market is moving away from it, surely the producers should be looking at the trend more closely.
Mr. Speaker, may I raise another point of concern? The people in my riding are most concerned about Toronto International Airport which borders the riding. Hardly a week goes by without some controversy arising about the airport. The question is asked, shall the airport remain as it is; should another runway be built, or should a second airport in the Toronto area be built? In 1968, the government decided that instead of building a fourth runway at Toronto International Airport, it would build a second airport in the Toronto area. I submit that the building of a fourth runway should not be
October 18, 1976

considered at this time, a suggestion strongly supported by all elected municipal councillors in the area, representatives in the provincial legislature, including the Premier of Ontario, and the four federal members representing constituencies surrounding the airport. We all want to know, what is to happen? What is to be the future of the second airport in the Toronto area?
I understand that the Ministry of Transport considered carefully several suitable sites and, having narrowed the choice to half a dozen, consulted the Ontario government as to which of those would be most suitable in the light of the growth the Ontario government forecast for Ontario. In the end Pickering was chosen. The government announced that it would proceed with Pickering airport. The intention was not to build the airport and then look for business; rather it was intended to build new facilities in accordance with demand. Unfortunately, the Ontario government later withdrew its support for the construction of Pickering airport. Now, all members from the Toronto area are concerned about the adequacy of Toronto's airport facilities in the future. Ten years from now will they be adequate?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the opportunity to speak in the throne speech debate I feel is most important, in light of the performance of this government during the past few years and, more particularly, the amazing disregard shown in the Speech from the Throne for some of the basic problems facing the country today. I enter this debate at a time when economic and social depression afflicts many people in specific areas and, indeed, whole regions of this country. This is a time of economic instability when the people of those areas need protection and assistance more than ever. At a time when the government should be highly visible and active in guaranteeing those needs, we are faced with an abdication of leadership by this government. Nowhere is this more obvious than in the recently delivered Speech from the Throne.
The Address-Mr. David MacDonald
The commitment of this government to regional development which, in my view, has always been more rhetorical than real, has disappeared almost entirely as a result of the total absence of leadership we see today. Neglect, insensitivity and inconsistency with regard to regional disparity haunts almost every move of the economic and social performance of this government.
In words that are now bitterly prophetic, the former leader of my party, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), warned of dangers ahead in the fight against disparity. Speaking on second reading of the bill which created in 1969 the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, more than seven years ago, he said that it might, in effect, allow other ministers to say "Let Jean do it" and not accept any particular responsibility for or even wash their hands of, the whole problem of regional disparity. I know it will bring him little joy to note that his words, to my mind, have come true with a vengeance. On occasions far too numerous to mention many members, not only on my side of the House, have reminded successive ministers of the department, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself, that the task of dealing effectively with regional disparities in this country will not be achieved solely by programs coming under the responsibility of a minister of regional economic expansion. I submit that the names of the ministers who have been given that responsibility in this government read like a roll call of those guilty of dishonour, neglect, missed opportunities, shocking insensitivity, ignorance and even indifference toward the chronic needs of our disadvantaged regions.
I believe almost every minister has important responsibilities which affect either the bias in our structure which perpetuates underdevelopment or the opportunities for some regions to break free of their dependence and become once again self-sustaining members in the Canadian community. I propose today to review, for hon. members of this House, the work of various ministries, from the standpoint of the way in which their performance has undermined and made almost meaningless the work done by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion under various ministers and numerous officials.
When I speak of an inconsistency of approach, perhaps I should say that no minister reflects this inconsistency better than does the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). There is little doubt in the minds of our poorer communities, east, west and centre, who should head the list. The minister has made it obvious to us, with his user-pay policy, that in no way is he prepared to support or even understand the concept of regional economic development. I am not sure whether in adopting the user-pay concept, the Minister of Transport is haunted by the ghost of the MacPherson commission report of the 1960s, the ideas of Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, who established the terms of reference of the new Canadian Transport Commission and then proceeded to become head of that commission, or by the ideas of the present head of the commission. Be that as it may, I believe that, in a basic way, the minister fails to understand how essential transportation policy is to this country's unity. It has been absolutely shocking to hear what the Minister of

The Address-Mr. David MacDonald Transport has said both inside and outside the Elouse about the responsibilities of his portfolio. If the minister had been in the position to exercise his user-pay policy during the tenure of this country's first government, the minister's own constituency would still be nothing more than a colony of prairie dogs. Fortunately, Sir John A. Macdonald did not adopt a policy of user-apay with respect to the railroads, railroads which the minister well knows have been basically important to the opening up and development of his own home area.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

speechtext: You are distorting his position, David.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I should be delighted to hear the Minister of Transport speak about the way in which transport policy favours regional development initiatives. I say this as it was incredible to me that, not many months ago, the minister saw fit to make, as part of his package of restraints, 53 per cent of his restraint cutbacks at the expense of Atlantic Canada alone. Let the parliamentary secretary explain that as an aspect in support of regional development. When I think that in the past year we have had rail freight increases between Atlantic Canada and Ontario in the order of 85 per cent, I wonder how this minister or parliamentary secretary can in any way justify the statement that they are contributing to the alleviation of regional disparities, trying to bring the country together in a more united and equitable fashion.
I have only a relatively brief period of time to catalogue all the sins of omission and commission of the Minister of Transport because there are a number of other ministries that obviously must be traced as well. I will deal with as many as I have time for in the brief period available. I want to raise one 1 am sure is of interest to the hon. member opposite. I refer to the responsibilities and the performance of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). The minister's pricing policy for fuel wiped out more family savings in a single winter in Atlantic Canada than the depression and prohibition combined. His contingency plan, in the face of maritimers selling their homes because they could not afford to heat them, consisted of attacking provincial administrations. A newsletter from the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council of a few months ago pointed to high energy prices as an obvious possible cause for continuing disparity.
It is a difficult point to argue when you know, for example, that a commercial firm in Charlottetown last winter paid twice as much for its energy, electricity, as its counterpart in Ontario. It is difficult as well to argue when a consumer in Toronto is paying 4.8 per cent of his income for energy costs compared to a homeowner in my province who paid 12 per cent of his income for energy last winter.
The minister persists in his myopic claim that the high prices are necessary to energy conservation, although consumption in Atlantic Canada is as low as two thirds of the national average. Somehow he is determined to make that disadvantaged region pay dearly for wasteful habits that are not of its own making. The lack of awareness and insensitivity

of this minister is frightening. There was not a single mention of the Atlantic energy problem in the Speech from the Throne. As recently as last Friday, my colleague, the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), raised with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources what response will be coming from the federal government with regard to the urgent request from Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island for substantial temporary aid by way of subsidy in connection with their serious problems in meeting excessively high energy costs. The minister replied, and I quote:
I have nothing new to add on this question. The matter is under continuing study at the present time.
That is the level of interest and action on the part of this minister. It is not untypical of a number of his colleagues as well. There are questions and issues that must be resolved. Some were raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates), who in speaking in this debate on Friday mentioned the need for action with regard to the continuing possibility and potential of Fundy tidal power. There was no mention of assistance to provinces trying to convert away from their reliance on petroleum for energy. The government of my province placed proposals before this government months ago, but still no reply. There was no mention of any initiatives to equalize the costs of electrical power for business and industry across Canada. There was nothing which might show some glimmer of understanding on the part of the minister that energy costs must not be permitted to widen the disparity gap even further. I will leave the Minister of Energy there, even though there is much more that could and should be said.
With the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), we move from an area of insensitivity to obvious flippancy. In February of this year, the Minister of Finance was asked what effective measures he was prepared to implement in response to the growing disparity in unemployment rates between the various regions. His answer to this House was that he had at least decided not to take the suggestion offered by someone that DREE be cancelled. What a farce. What insensitivity. Earlier this year, during the energy crunch faced by many disadvantaged regions, we asked the minister what differential in energy rates he was prepared to allow before taking remedial steps. Not only had he not given the matter consideration, he had no intention of doing so. When we consider some of the agencies under this minister's jurisdiction, such as the Federal Business Development Bank which has a lower loan loss write-off than even the chartered banks, we wonder what little difference it can possibly make with regard to the alleviation of regional disparities.
The minister has at least been honest about his attitude toward the poorer regions, insensitive as that may be. He was the one who went on record to admit, frankly and brutally, that his government was not going to do anything to help the areas of chronic depression during a time of government restraint. Indeed, he made remarks to suggest that it would almost be inappropriate to take into account the regional

variations that exist within this country with respect to the government's overall restraint program.
I could and should say more about the Minister of Finance, but I want to move to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). The Minister of Agriculture was given a very significant message from, of all places, the other place. In a report from the Senate on the situation in Kent County, New Brunswick, the minister should have received a message, loud and clear. I had hoped he would be here to hear this message in case he did not hear it earlier.
The Senate report describes the stifling practices of the Department of Agriculture which attempt to force areas such as Kent County into the mold of national policies which are neither designed for, appropriate to or wanted by its citizens. The report exposes the "big or bust" bias which runs through the programs of Agriculture Canada, singling out the Farm Credit Corporation and the unfortunately or misappropriately named Small Farm Development Program for their discrimination against the small-scale farmer. It reports, and I find this almost hard to believe, the callous refusal of one of the officials of Agriculture Canada to grant a loan with the words that, and I quote:
Kent County is not profitable, there is no future there.
I hope the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) have an opportunity to discuss that report. I would be delighted to be a silent listener in that tete-a-tete. There is also the impact of this minister's supply-management programs to consider, and there was some discussion of that in the question period today, whose quotas lock the Atlantic region into a permanent status of net food importers.
The Senate study I just mentioned is backed up on this point by a report of the Economic Council of Canada on regional unemployment which points out how the need to bring in foodstuffs costs the region 11,000 jobs. What maritime agriculture needs, says the Senate report, and this is obvious to many people, is development, and not stabilization. Even though he is not here at this time, I trust that the Minister of Agriculture will have an opportunity to learn again these basic truths.
I leave the minister there with his homework to do and I turn my attention to the President of Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). We find a new minister there but, again, whether it is a new minister or an old minister we are dealing with the same old gang which took the view in December of last year as well as in the previous period of restraint five or six years ago, that the government could not reallocate moneys within the various programs and departments to ease the load on provinces which were suffering from high, chronic unemployment, because it was not something the government had either the imagination or the will to do. Frankly, with supporters like this, one wonders why the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) even bothers to stay at the job.
I want to mention the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) because I do not want him to feel
The Address-Mr. David MacDonald neglected. I am sure he is aware of the attention drawn by Dr. Raynauld of the Economic Council of Canada to the large productivity gap which exists between workers in various regions of our country. Yet to my knowledge the hon. gentleman's department continues to give priority to productivity incentives for the high technology industries, not the labourintensive needs of the poorer communities.
I would expect as well in his department a high priority in the trade division to finding markets based on the potential of those communities and I would have hoped-falsely I suspect-that prior to the GATT negotiations a special review would have been undertaken of those tariffs of ours and of foreign countries which would have a direct bearing on regional development. I regret, however, to say I have seen no evidence of either. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, even his colleague who formerly occupied that office and who had also been Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, fails to see regional economic expansion as part of his responsibility. This shows, I guess, the kind of watertight compartment in which regional development has finally been placed.
When we think of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), we recall what has been said about developing a population policy to encourage young people, the active and dynamic elements of our society. Is this policy to be related to a long-term program designed to alleviate regional disparity? Not a word about this aspect. How can the Speech from the Throne promise an immigration policy sensitive to regional needs when the minister's own predecessor admitted to me in correspondence last summer that there were no studies and, apparently, little concern with respect to the effect of immigration on local or regional economies.
There are so many other ministers, Mr. Speaker, that obviously there would not be the opportunity to spend a modicum of time discussing their shortfalls with respect to supporting the so-called basic commitment of the government to reducing regional disparity. When we think of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan), we wonder what input is taken into account in relation to public works expenditures as they affect regional development. I ask the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner) how much of the funding under his responsibility has aided research and development relative to the needs of small-scale technology in certain regions of this country or whether this aspect was even considered, much less given priority? I ask the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) whether the awarding of contracts has been related to the specific needs or potential of various areas in this country? There is a long catalogue of insensitivity, lack of awareness and neglect which involves every minister of the government. It is obvious no attempt has been made to exercise responsibility along the lines of the theme announced in successive Speeches from the Throne and in the course of speeches made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself.
Before I deal with the Prime Minister-

speechtext: Before I leave all the other ministers, let me say that in no way do I wish to excuse successive ministers of regional economic expansion or absolve the department from responsibility for the lack of commitment to regional equality. Under a minister who seems half-hearted at best about his task, afraid to speak out-

-and a department which seems mainly concerned about protecting its own empire, I am not surprised that other departments have felt neither the urge nor the pressure to tackle disparity. The department has obviously failed to take the lead in co-ordinating the activities of other federal departments though the first minister himself stated on a number of occasions that such co-ordination was vital to the success of DREE.
Then again, there has obviously been lack of co-ordination with respect to the attitude of the department toward the various priorities established by the provinces. According to a study produced this year, there are today more than 200 different federal and provincial incentive programs for industry. Surely, one might expect DREE to take the lead in bringing some measure of rationality to these policies in place of the confusion and contradiction which presently exists according to the study I have mentioned. I wonder, too, why successive ministers have been negligent in building a commitment to regional development right across the country among rich and poor areas alike. I say this because in the absence of grass roots support the minister will never get the close co-operation from his colleagues which is vital to success.
I have no time to deal specifically, now, with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion; I know that some of my hon. friends wish to do so. However, I do wish to say to the minister-and I am glad he is present to hear these words- that his failure to indicate the prospect of any amendment of the Regional Development Incentives Act in the Speech from the Throne cannot pass unnoticed. As hon. members will recall, I asked him last week to explain this ominous silence. His answer to me that his officials were beginning to consider this particular matter showed, in my estimation, a shocking disregard for one of the basic programs under his jurisdiction.
What I have in mind, now, are not radical or major changes. Nevertheless, suggestions for changes have been made and need to be implemented. They have come from a variety of sources including the hon. gentleman's own Atlantic Development Council which has recommended streamlined procedures, post-incentive assistance, monitoring and other arrangements which might allow the government to take an equity position in certain new ventures. Economists, too, have studied the program and pointed out some of its defects, such as the capital bias of the grants system. I know the minister is aware of these comments. He did not take office last week, or a month ago, or six months ago. He has been hearing constructive comments and amendments almost from the time RDIA was put into effect, and that was to be expected. What is not expected is that the minister and his officials should adopt

such a cavalier approach in face of the amendments which are obviously required if the program is to be successful. I believe the Atlantic Council when it said in its report that the RDIA program "does not appear to have any readily discernible effect upon the relative growth performance of the manufacturing sector in the Atlantic provinces." In these circumstances I would have expected more urgency in the minister's behaviour.

Mr. Speaker, before lunch I had dwelt at some length on the failure of a series of ministers within this administration to support the over-all concept of the alleviation of regional disparities in this country. Perhaps members on all sides wonder why I have spent almost all my time in this speech dealing with this particular aspect. I have done so, quite frankly, because I took the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at his word. I took him at his word when in 1968 he promised a Marshall plan for the maritimes. He told us that the perpetuation of regional inequality meant, to quote him, "that the unity of this country is almost as surely destroyed as it would be by the French-English confrontation". It is he who, in his almost complete failure to match rhetoric with action, has denied this government and the country the leadership, the sense of urgency, that would have required each single department and agency of his government to make regional development central to its responsibility and concern. It is true that regional disparity has been with us for some time. But from the time the Prime Minister assumed the leadership in 1968 he has on repeated occasions made that kind of commitment. I should like to quote from an article that he wrote in 1969 which appeared in the Atlantic Advocate. He said:
That is why I have begun by trying to make clear the central place that regional development occupies in the whole thinking about the future of Canada-
No commitment could be clearer than that. In light of the commitments that have been made by the Prime Minister and referred to from time to time in speeches from the throne since he has occupied that office, it is inconceivable that there would not be a total commitment on the part of all departments. Yet obviously this has not been so.
I think we must learn at least two or three lessons from the experience that we have been through during the last seven years. Genuine and effective regional development cannot be compartmentalized. If this government has proved anything since it assumed office-if I may refer to my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Stanfield)-it is that "Let John do it" will not work. Neither will it work when we say "Let Marcel do it" or, for that matter, any other minister who might occupy responsibility for that department. I think Canadians have realized
October 18, 1976

during the performance of this government that there must be a total approach to a realistic alleviation of regional disparities. I think it is clear that one cannot go somewhere unless one knows where he is going. What does that mean? Let me quote from a report of a few years back, 1971, of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council in their Fifth Annual Review of the Atlantic Economy. In their conclusions and recommendations they said:
What is needed from DREE are specific goals and targets, benchmarks by which it may judge, and be judged, on its performance.
APEC was not the only body calling in the early years or since for some clearly defined set of goals, perhaps both long-term and short-term. It was not the only body which suggested it would not be good enough just to have some generally good intentions without a strategy to achieve those goals. Clearly, from the outset in 1969 until the present date we have not had that.
Third, I think it is quite obvious that regional policies and programs will be merely patchwork and inconsistent without an over-all national policy and framework. Perhaps the main reason we have not had an effective regional development experience in this country is there has been lack of an over-all framework of goals in terms of a national policy. The difference, quite clearly, in the approach of this government and the approach we are taking is summed up in the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) when he spoke in Charlottetown a little over three weeks ago and said:
The problem is that regional disparity is an issue on the fringes of government policy-making, instead of being a preoccupation at the centre of government policy-making, where it should be and where it will be in a Progressive Conservative government. Regional disparity is not a DREE problem, as Mr. Trudeau would have it. It is a national problem. Concern for regional problems must permeate national energy policy... must underlie national transport policy ... must inform the whole field of the federal-provincial relations, and must be a prime consideration in the formulation of the fiscal and economic policy of the government.
This is the intent; this is the spirit; this is the direction in which we must move if we are ever to deal with what the Prime Minister has referred to as one of the twin problems that threatens Canadian unity and, indeed, Canadian confederation.

Mr. Speaker, may I open by joining others in this House in offering my congratulations to the new and young members of the House who moved and seconded the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) and the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance). Also, along with other hon. members I wish to mention our deep regret at the passing of our colleague, a marvellous woman with great dedication, sincerity and a very considerable degree of strength and firmness, all wrapped up in a great deal of charm. Of course, I refer to Madam Morin, our esteemed colleague from Louis-Hebert who left us recently and left a great deal of sadness behind her.
The Address-Mr. Andras
In entering this debate, may I say that it has not been my custom or style to emulate the bombast with which the opposition invariably fills Hansard on such occasions, so I think I shall allow the gibbering wit and witless jibes with which the opposition members approached the Speech from the Throne to stand for what they represent, an empty response to a comprehensive government program designed to strengthen national unity, enhance equality of opportunity and redefine the role of government in consultation and co-operation with the private sector so that we can as a society and as a nation better fulfil the present and future needs of our people.
As we say in the other official language, "gouverner c'est prevoir". The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) last week told us-or taxed us, indeed-with opportunism because we rejected what I can only call his myopic perceptions of the current problems of the country because we are determined to continue our search for durable solutions to the pervasive and complex problems, whether they be inflation, labour unrest, linguistic tensions or, as referred to by my hon. friend from Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), the problems of regional disparities. Certainly, the Leader of the Opposition is dazzled, I guess, by his own ambitions in that he proclaimed this very weekend that the government had lost the will to govern, presumably because we intend to propose to the House at this session an exhaustive series of co-ordinated measures to improve the social framework for public and private initiative, to raise the productivity performance of all the economic agents with which we have to deal, and to enable all individual Canadians to achieve higher levels of self-fulfilment.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has shown his true colours, and when the ultimate poll is in, I think in a couple of years, his remarks will be seen for what they are, a dull and pretty stark etching of what I can only describe as inveterate pessimism.
The functions of Treasury Board as a central agency are so varied and so pervasive that I could speak and expound on virtually all or every aspect of the Speech from the Throne. But as I have just said, the debate on the address provides members with the unique opportunity to show their true colours, and in order to show mine for what they truly are, I will confine myself and my comments, after some preliminary remarks, to an aspect of public service management which recently has caused some apprehension in the country, namely, the pensions of federal public servants and then I want to move on to an issue of grave national concern, which is the government's official languages policy.
The overriding preoccupation of Treasury Board, of course, throughout this session will be to ensure that the expenditures of the federal government do not exceed the growth trend of the gross national product and that substantial, visible and perceptible progress is made toward improving the efficiency, the effectiveness and sensitivity of the public service. I intend to be absolutely brutal with regard to wasteful spending
158

October 18, 1976
The Address-Mr. Andras
practices and, indeed, very tough on the monetary control of overhead expenditures.
1 know this may not please some public servants. For instance, they will now have to account for such things as the taxi slips they use in the course of their work. But they must understand that they are accountable to the public for every dollar they legitimately spend on such activities and, indeed, that effective monitoring is necessary to discipline the very few who in the past were not averse to taking a free ride at the expense of the taxpayers. I mention taxis, not because I expect great savings from the new procedure but because this is a highly visible example of the type of administrative overhead cost which we are determined to bring under tighter control.
On program expenditures, the government intends to pursue the efforts begun during the first phase of the restraint program to curb the growth of outlays and improve their cost-effectiveness, while maintaining and even improving the quality of public goods and services provided to Canadians. One of the great architects of this century, Mies van de Rohe, used to say "Less is more" when some customer objected to his ruthless suppression of unnecessary embellishments from contemporary designs. That, I think, is what I will adopt as my motto at the Treasury Board. But I want to say I am very convinced that public expenditures can be restrained in a socially progressive way and without paralysing program innovations and expansions.
That conviction, too, will be one of the guiding principles of the Treasury Board in its attempt to find and stick to the middle road charted by the Speech from the Throne and, of course, to assist other departments and agencies in relying more on the private sector to achieve their social and economic objectives. To those ends, the Treasury Board will continue to extend its fullest co-operation to the Auditor General. Indeed, legislation will soon be introduced to clarify the duties and responsibilities of that officer of parliament and to provide him with better means of fulfilling his very important functions.
I will have more to say later in the session on the government's determination to bring down the rate of growth of the public service from 1 Vi per cent to less than 1 per cent in the next fiscal year, and similarly to contain the growth of the senior executive complement.
As stated in the throne speech, the government also intends to improve the working conditions and the collective bargaining system in the public service, notably to try to reduce the adversary nature of that process and to ensure an equitable relationship between compensation levels in the public as compared to the private sector. I do not intend to allow the public service to become the scapegoat. At the same time, I expect public servants to be aware at all times that they serve the government and that the government is accountable to the Canadian taxpayers for the work that they do, for the compensation that they get and for the conditions of employment they enjoy.

The Treasury Board will continue to be a good employer and public servants who pull their weight will be adequately rewarded. Others who do not will find that the federal government is going to become a less comfortable environment. The Treasury Board will continue to honour all commitments made in the collective bargaining framework, but certainly it will insist that public service bargaining agents also honour their commitments.
These general policies in the management of the public service will apply to an area which, as I said earlier, has generated a considerable amount of public attention, and indeed criticism over the past year, namely, the pension arrangements that have been established for federal public servants. The government has taken these concerns most seriously, and it requested about a year ago that the Treasury Board secretariat undertake a general review of the public service pension plan, first to ascertain the facts, and at a later stage to determine what adjustments, if any, should be considered. The first stage of this review has been completed and I tabled a document this morning in the House which outlined the preliminary conclusions and many of the facts on which these preliminary conclusions are based.

On this occasion I will not attempt to summarize the document which has been made available to all in the House and to the general public. I would like to point out, however, that much of the recent discussion of the public service pension plan has ignored a major factor, perhaps the key factor, in trying to explain why public servants are receiving what we will admit are above average retirement benefits, that is, that the public servants themselves make above average contributions to their pension plan. In other words, public servants have themselves decided that generally they are willing to defer a higher proportion of their current income than other groups of employees in Canada. They will get more later, but they pay more now.
1 want to make it quite clear that the document I tabled does not express the definitive view of the government on public service pensions, because that program, like others, is kept under continuing review. A number of developments will give us an opportunity to reassess its provisions in the near future. I am referring in particular to the comprehensive review of the pension policy which will be conducted jointly by the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Finance.
1 turn now to another key element in the Speech from the Throne, namely, the government's official languages policy. By way of introduction to that subject, allow me to say that I deeply regret the untimely departure from the cabinet of the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) for whom 1 have considerable personal regard and whom I have known for a long time. I regret even more some of the reasons he put forward to explain his resignation from the cabinet.

October 18, 1976

I do not intend to comment on the government's often stated intention to achieve formal constitutional independence, the modalities of which have not yet been defined and can only be defined after detailed consultations with the provinces. All I can say is that there is no plot, no secret plan, no conspiracy afoot to bring the constitution home. The government has not operated that way, and indeed if it ever did 1 would no longer be a part of it.
Moreover, this government will never lock into the constitution the specifics, the details of any federal policy or program as opposed to the fundamental principles of law, for the simple reason that those kinds of specific details, policies and programs must be subject to continuous adjustment and improvement. But I do wish to state categorically that in my view this country will not survive if federal policies are designed, or perceived as being designed, to placate or to contain any particular region, province or group until such time as it achieves what some people have decreed as its proper place within the Canadian federation. That applies as much to Quebec on language rights as to the western provinces on resource policies, to Ontario on industrial issues or to the Atlantic provinces on regional development.
The conviction that Canada is more than the sum of its constituent parts, that the national interest is more than the lowest common denominator between the interests of various regions, is crucial to the continued existence of this country. As stated in the Speech from the Throne, that need not and should not lead to rigid uniformity, but it does require that all federal policies be designed to reflect and promote the interests of all Canadians wherever they happen to live. That has been, and will continue to be, the case for the official languages policy.
I also wish to state categorically that commitment to linguistic equality, like commitment to equality before the law, equality of opportunity and other democratic rights, cannot be meted out to the citizenry in great or small doses depending on whim and fancy. The ways and means to ensure these rights which are enjoyed to the fullest extent by all citizens should, of course, be under continuing review and should be continually improved. Laws can be changed, policies adjusted and programs overhauled, but equality is either recognized and proclaimed or it does not exist.

Seven years ago in this House parliament did recognize and did proclaim equality of the two official languages of Canada. That historic act was promulgated with the support of all political parties represented in the House. The validity of the act was confirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada. It is the view of the government that there cannot, and should not be, any backtracking from the fundamental provisions of that legislation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated a couple of years ago, in 1974, the determination of the government to make linguistic equality an irreversible fact of Canadian life by the end of this decade, and I endorse that goal without any reservation whatsoever. In my view we
The Address-Mr. Andras
simply cannot afford the "wait and see" approach which has been suggested-I am sure with the best intentions-by the hon. member for Winnipeg South.
While listening to the speech made last Wednesday by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), I was relieved to note that he apparently shares the views of the government on this question, and 1 can only hope that his position is supported by all members of his caucus. However, I must take issue with his charge that the current uneasiness in the country about the official languages policy and program is attributable only to errors made in the course of their implementation, particularly in the federal public service. I suggest that the discontent and doubts recently expressed by many Canadians also reflect our inability as politicians to explain to these Canadians the true intent and nature of our languages policy and to demonstrate to them its essential fairness and reasonableness. I further suggest that in this respect English-speaking members on both sides of this House must take their full share of the blame.

I do not want to be misunderstood on this issue. I am not trying to pass the buck. Errors have been made, and that must be admitted. They have to be acknowledged, and they are going to be corrected. But given the experimental nature of many of the programs devised to implement the Official Languages Act and the parliamentary resolution of 1973, I think it was probably inevitable that specific aspects of these programs might prove to be less effective three or five years after their introduction than was originally expected, and certainly a contrary situation would have been surprising. Even the best thought-out government programs must periodically be adjusted to take into account the lessons of experience, the change in circumstances or advances in human knowledge. As the former minister of manpower and immigration, hon. members may recognize that I speak on that subject with some experience and authority.
It also must be pointed out that in our efforts to convert the public service of Canada into a functionally bilingual institution, without hampering its effectiveness and without prejudicing the career entitlements of public servants already on strength, we could not rely on the experience of other countries since it was, by and large, a task of unprecedented magnitude which had to be tailored, and still must be tailored, to specific Canadian requirements.
Both my predecessor and I have indicated in very recent months that a comprehensive review of all linguistic policies and programs is under way, and the government has pledged in the Speech from the Throne that those programs which have been successful will be continued, while those which have not will be modified. I can already assure the House, for example, that language training programs will be improved, that the linguistic requirements of positions will be reidentified, and that language standards will be revised. As a personal note, I might say that I am as intrigued, as I think my

predecessor was, by the concept of receptive bilingualism as opposed to active or complete proficiency in both official languages, because it may often correspond more accurately to the practical requirements of functional bilingualism in the public service.
The House will be informed in the course of this session of the government's decisions on specific issues in this area. However, in view of their often stated interest in and their criticism of the implementation of the Official Languages Act,
I advise opposition members that in many areas we have not completed our review and I welcome and invite them to give us their ideas before we come to definite conclusions. Indeed, those kinds of suggestions will be more than welcome. However, no matter how much we adjust and readjust our program, we will not succeed in building a durable national consensus on official languages unless we manage to convince all Canadians-particularly, nowadays, English-speaking Canadians-that federal policies in this field do derive from fundamental principles of justice, equality and tolerance which should apply everywhere, in western Canada as well as in Quebec and in Ontario as well as in the Atlantic region. In that respect, the mere possibility of failure has frightening implications and for that reason I suggest that the task at hand should mobilize the elected representatives of all parties from all regions of Canada.
In recent months I have come to the conclusion that both parliament and the government have very much underestimated the need for facts and for public information on official languages policies, most particularly in English Canada. I do not think Canadians are more bigoted or intolerant-in fact, they are probably less so-than people anywhere else in the world. The mosaic of our nation indicates that to me. However, I do feel that because our French-speaking population- six million people, more than the combined population of the prairie provinces, most of whom are unilingual-is so heavily concentrated in the province of Quebec, it has been very difficult, as it was for me when I first came out of the west to parliament eleven years ago, for a great number of people to perceive the need for this policy, for the simple reason that they live in regions of the country where there are few French-speaking Canadians.
I think, also, that many people, particularly outside Quebec-and I think this is where we have fallen down-have not been made aware of the true and limited implications of the official languages policy for them because those implications are minimal. I think those people have too often been left with the impression that the policy grants special privileges to the French language and somehow diminishes the proper and necessary status of the English language in the federal government, and of course that really is nonsense.
However, the fact is that we have tended to take public opinion for granted on this issue. More often than not-and in Canada I believe it is necessary to correct this now-I think we have failed to recognize the normal anxieties of Englishspeaking Canadians. After all, they are not superhuman. We have neglected to repeat often enough and patiently enough
[Mr. Andras.1
the converse of what our French-speaking colleagues have been saying to their constituents for years. They have been saying, first, that the Official Languages Act entrenches the right of English-speaking Canadians to deal with the federal government in English, to work for federal departments and agencies in that language and to learn the other official language only if they wish to do so.
Second, they have been saying that the official languages policy has effectively recognized the distinct personality and the different needs of each region, so that in the four western provinces, for example, over 98 per cent of the federal public service positions require only knowledge of English from their incumbents for the simple reason that the need for a bilingual capacity in federal offices located there is minimal.
Third, through the whole the public service today only about 20 per cent of the positions are identified as bilingual, and 87 per cent of these are located in areas of the country where there is an obvious need for them. I am talking about the national capital region, metropolitan Montreal, northern and eastern Ontario and northern and eastern New Brunswick.
Fourth, the conditional appointment and language training programs for bilingual positions, which is the most expensive and the most often criticized aspect of our policies, were specifically designed to enable all Canadians from all parts of Canada to compete for jobs identified as bilingual even if the applicants were unilingual; and so on.
We have not got that kind of story across. We believed that the facts would speak for themselves, but unfortunately they have not. The fact that many Canadians still think that the government is trying to ram French down their throats is indicative of our failure to communicate these facts to the public because, I repeat, the Official Languages Act was adopted precisely to achieve and preserve freedom of choice for all Canadians with respect to our official languages.
Despite the fact that I am unilingual, for instance, and that my political roots are in Ontario, that I was brought up in western Canada and that I have lived in most regions of English Canada, these facts make me confident that the current disenchantment of English-speaking Canadians with respect to bilingualism can be dissipated. I certainly intend to give top priority to public information on that subject as part of my responsibilities. I am unilingual, and although I regret that very much, I do not have great hang-ups about it. I can honestly say that I have not suffered because of it since I came to Ottawa 11 years ago.
I think that is the way it should be, although I am very well aware that for some federal public servants, most of them French Canadians but more recently a certain number of Anglophones, unilingualism has been a handicap. I cannot claim to have a great facility for languages, but I can tell the House that I have tried, and still try, to acquire a receptive capacity in the French language. I know I shall never be able to make a resounding speech in Quebec like the Prime Minister or the hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Marchand).

May I convey through you, Mr. Speaker, my gratitude to the House. This leads me to look at the "youth option" recommended by the Commissioner of Official Languages and which, in the Speech from the Throne, the government has accepted in principle. I believe there is a lot of evidence that although they have some reservations about some of our linguistic programs, Canadians are particularly anxious that their children have the best possible chance of understanding their compatriots in the other language. Accordingly, we as a government are going to discuss with the provinces arrangements to increase the effectiveness of official languages training in the country's school systems.
My personal experience makes me particularly sympathetic to the difficulties faced by unilingual public servants-and I am talking about unilingual public servants of both languages. In undertaking my new responsibilities, I certainly intend to see that these difficulties are very carefully examined and that programs and procedures are reviewed in order to minimize them and, wherever possible, eliminate them.
At the same time, I am taking steps to ensure that my unilingualism in the Treasury Board does not cause a reversal of the very considerable progress made under my predecessors to make French an effective working language within the Treasury Board secretariat. About 20 per cent or 30 per cent of the secretariat's internal working papers are currently drafted in French, and I intend to maintain the proportion. I think it is incumbent upon Treasury Board to be a leading agency in this area. It is my ambition to show how a unilingual minister can adjust to functional bilingualism in the public service of Canada. I am winding down to the conclusion of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, and unfortunately recent events require that I conclude on a more sombre note.
The Address-Mr. Andras
Passion has run high and tensions are mounting; pronouncements have ranged from the outlandish to the extravagant. Only last week I saw on the front page of Le Devoir an article by the editor in chief who is obviously dismayed about these outbursts on official languages and French-English relations. While he came down on the right side, his comments gave rise to the headline which asked whether Canada wanted to separate from Quebec. The notion entertained by some people that we should go through a replay of the battle of the Plains of Abraham over the Official Languages Act is an extremely dangerous delusion.
Our language development policy has nothing to do-and God forbid that it should-with the imperial rivalries between French and English of centuries ago. It stems from the concern for human rights and social justice which is surely a Canadian thing. It is a vital element of Canadian democracy. It is a necessary condition, and I say it is a practical requirement for effective and harmonious political association between two linguistic communities which simply cannot afford, in this day and age, to be "warring within the bosom of a single state", to paraphrase Lord Durham's famous report. Consequently, linguistic equality is one of the cornerstones of Canadian national unity.
To allow intercommunal conflict to develop over the language issue, as is currently threatened, would be a tragic case of self-destruction for this country. English Canadians could not win that battle. French Canadians could not be brought to defeat on the contemporary battleground occupied by the separatist movement in Quebec. Canadians of other ethnic origins-the third group, as we sometimes call them-could not escape unscathed from such a conflict, because at the very root of it is intolerance. Intolerance would be the dominant passion, and I suggest that Canadians of other ethnic origins are particularly vulernable to intolerance. All would lose, and what would be lost would be Canada itself, the country our forebears built up and left to us in trust, a country which I think it is our moral and constitutional obligation to pass on to our children, strengthened and united.
I do not want to be of the generation that would allow fractious and disruptive forces to undermine the life of this country. I do not ever want to hear my children or two grandchildren say or even have them think in terms of, "You knew it was coming; you knew why, and you failed to prevent it." Those sentiments should apply to everyone in this House. It has for many years been my overriding concern, as it ought to be the concern of all here, that because of inaction or irresponsible action we should deserve to have such an indictment levelled at us by those who placed their trust in us: I was going to say "placed their trust in the government," but I really mean parliament.
That is why the Speech from the Throne announced a series of co-ordinated measures to strengthen national unity, expand individual freedom and enhance quality of opportunity. That is why the government is pledged to promoting better under-

The Address-Mr. Roche
standing between French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians. Personal conviction, as much as political commitment and ministerial responsibility, compel me to dedicate myself to the promotion of that understanding and to the building of a national consensus on official languages.
