speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak of Canada's role in the crisis of the United Nations. Judging by the throne speech, which devoted only four paragraphs to international affairs, not many Canadians appear to be interested in events beyond our borders. This myopic view of the government short-changes the Canadian public who have a right to much better leadership in pursuing a policy of enlightened internationalism.
We have a new Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) and I wish him well. It should not detract from the sincerity of my good wishes to him personally to express my wonder at how the nations of the world are to be expected to take Canada seriously when external affairs ministers are shifted because the government needs someone to find the way through the House of Commons. Is Canada's role internationally so unimportant, is the external affairs portfolio so simple that ministers can be switched in a political game of musical chairs?
The former external affairs minister was beginning to make his mark-especially as co-chairman of the north-south conference on international economic co-operation-after a two-year settling-in process, and I respected him. But how can we respect a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who forces his external affairs minister to vacate his office for, of all posts, the House leadership, thus upsetting the continuity of foreign policy. I cannot imagine Lester Pearson ever doing such a thing.
Of course we must go on not only developing but implementing a policy of realism in our relations with the global community. As we examine our fundamental policy of pursuing peace, I want to emphasize that through the United Nations Canada can make a major contribution to world order and peace in the last quarter of this century. There is a desperate need for fresh leadership at the UN and the moment is ripe. Canada has a new ambassador at the UN, in the skilled William Barton, and we are about to take a seat again on the security council.
The UN itself is changing. Certainly, the major task of the UN is still the maintenance of peace, "to save succeeding

generations from the scourge of war," as the founders of the UN expressed it. But the development of conditions of peace is now seen to require a wide range of activity: an equitable economic order, population control, an end to racial discrimination, a new law of the sea, a code of conduct for transnational corporations, protection of the environment, the development of human settlements. Global problems of the development of food, energy and jobs now dominate the UN agenda. A new Reader's Digest Gallup world public opinion poll reveals that the rich-poor disparity is now the dominant political fact on the planet. As Secretary General Kurt Waldheim puts it:
We have come to see that the security of this world is linked to an equitable sharing of wealth, not just as an objective for the distant future but as a matter of urgency.
The UN is making progress in solving the deeply human problems of world development. But at this very moment countless people are about to give up on the United Nations. That is why I said at the outset that there is a crisis of the United Nations. It is being subverted by those who are more strongly motivated by racial hatred than by the peaceful development of mankind. Anti-Jewish hatred nearly wrecked the Habitat conference in Vancouver last June. The very existence of UNESCO is threatened by the adamant refusal of the Arab-Communist bloc to allow Israel to join it. Prominent scientists and academics have called for an end to anti-Israel discrimination or face the possible collapse of UNESCO.
All people at the UN must find ways to stop the spread of racism in the conferences and resolutions that give the UN its image. Racism will destroy the credibility of the United Nations as an instrument of peace. Already that credibility is being questioned as never before. How can the UN be a moral force to stop the escalation of violation of human rights around the world if it is corroded by hatred from within?
As a politician strongly in support of more Canadian involvement in the UN, I am concerned about the growing public reaction against the UN on many fronts. It is attacked because it cannot stop local wars now going on. It cannot even agree on a formula to act against international terrorism; it is paralysed in advancing disarmament and cannot stop the spread of deadly nuclear fuel reprocessing plants. The General Assembly has become a bear-pit in which newly liberated third world nations trample on the old, industrialized nations. The good will of the west in advancing economic development is undermined by the politics of hate.
The media, feasting on confrontation, have put across the message of the UN as a force to be tolerated rather than a force to be supported. The combination of stupidities within the UN and the media's concentration on its failures rather than successes has resulted in the lowest public confidence in the UN's 31-year history. How is it that every Canadian knows about the infamous anti-Zionist resolution passed at the UN and hardly a handful know what the new international economic order is all about?
I count it a good day if I have persuaded a voter not to demand a cutback in Canada's support of the UN rather than
October 18, 1976

persuading him to support increased commitments. Canada pays 3 per cent of the UN budget. It has become all'too easy to vent our frustrations over future shock by scorning the UN as incomprehensible and irrelevant-as if it were easy to find agreement among 144 nations.
Although there are times when any thinking person must despair at the abuses and misuses of the United Nations, we must not lose light of the great achievements of the UN. Sometimes I hear the accusation, "Name me one good thing the UN has ever done." I can name many. The UN helps the homeless. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees has helped 200,000 displaced persons resettle in Africa, and 216,000 in Asia. The UN bridges the illiteracy gap. The United Nations' Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization has trained more than 64,000 teachers and educational planners in low income countries. The UN fights famine. By providing technical assistance and research, the Food and Agricultural Organization is promoting modern agricultural techniques, better plant strains, better irrigation and soil management, better food processing, storage and distribution.
The UN brings milk to the world's children. The United Nations' children's fund has helped to set up 220 milk processing plants in 45 countries for cheap and sanitary distribution of this important source of protein. The UN helps provide clean water. Nearly 90 per cent of rural populations in developing countries drink tainted water-a leading cause of sickness and death. The United Nations' environment program has mounted a drive with other international agencies to deliver safe, potable water. UNEP also keeps track of pollutants in the oceans, the atmosphere and on earth to provide scientists with an accurate picture of our planet's health. The United Nations helps people help themselves. Last year the United Nations development program sent more than 9,800 experts to work on 7,600 projects in 144 countries and territories.
These are only the highlights in a long catalogue of United Nations' accomplishments that we too often overlook. Most people think of the United Nations as only the general assembly and the security council. But a vital part of the United Nations, where more than 90 per cent of its budget goes, is this world wide system of specialized agencies and programs. We cannot properly assess the United Nations' role and potential in building global strategies for peace by looking only at the skirmishes in the spotlight. The United Nations must be related to the sweep of history passing before our eyes.
The past 30 years has been one of the most dangerous periods in human history. It was a period of Promethean change during which we ran the risks of several world wide conflagrations. North and south, east and west, rich and poor, black and white, the powerful and the weak, came into contact with each other under explosive circumstances.
Science and technology made incredible strides, for good and bad. Atomic weapons and energy were born. Man landed
The Address-Mr. Roche
on the moon. More than a thousand satellites were launched around the earth. Man further extended the power of his eyes with giant telescopes, spectroscopes, television, electronic microscopes and radars; the power of his hands with incredible machines and factories; the faculties of his hearing with sonars, radio and space telecommunications; the capacities of his brain with computers and automation. His knowledge has reached farther and farther into the universe and deeper and deeper into the infinitely small. Many of his inventions bore seeds of progress as well as of destruction. A world war was nevertheless avoided, and I believe that the United Nations has played an important role in building bridges and reducing tensions.
The changes of the past 30 years have revealed many limits and constraints regarding human life and behaviour on our planet: limits of population; limits of the environment, limits of growth, limits of resources, limits of the biosphere. These external constraints begin to demonstrate to governments that there are also limits to power. I believe that this first correct view of our planet and of human life on it, obtained in large degree through the United Nations and its specialized agencies, will finally bring governments to act in a more responsible and concerted way.
This evolutionary progress is the real value of UN work. With its 16 specialized agencies, 14 permanent programs and string of world conferences, the United Nations is working on the whole fabric of peace. The UN is helping us to know what we need to know to ensure a decent, peaceful and happy life of self-fulfilled people. National governments are learning that they must co-operate because of the physical and economic interdependence of the whole planet. The UN even in these early stages of its development, is one of the most astonishing instruments on earth. This is a time to praise it, not damn it.
As we consider a greater role for Canada in the global community, we must note the UN shift in emphasis from peacekeeping to international economic and social development. Peace is no longer defined as the absence of war; peace now means human development. Far from being different goals, peacekeeping and development should be intertwined in our total contribution to peace. Canada has consistently supported United Nations activities in maintaining peace and security. With 1,500 military personnel abroad in this capacity, Canada is the largest contributor of troops for UN peacekeeping. We can make an even greater contribution, in a military sense, by stepping up our efforts to end the arms race. Here the special qualifications of Ambassador Barton, formerly Canada's envoy to the UN disarmament committee, will be significant in intensifying Canada's work.
The UN Secretary-General considers the arms race to be "one of the most critical world problems that confronts us today." In a world increasingly preoccupied with the problems of social justice, hunger, poverty, illiteracy, disease, development and an equitable sharing of resources, world military expenditures have spiralled to $300 billion a year. By shameful contrast, the net flow of official development assistance is only $15 billion a year. The international arms trade has reached

October 18, 1976
The Address-Mr. Roche
$20 billion-including Canada's share-conventional weapons are becoming increasingly more sophisticated and deadly, and the technological arms race threatens to produce even more horrible means of mass destruction.
While some 400,000 engineers and scientists are working on military projects which absorb some 40 per cent of the funds allocated in the world to research and development, important problems facing mankind and requiring the contribution of those scientists and engineers are being neglected. The continued "improvement" of nuclear weapons that could obliterate all human life many times over is a demonic spectacle.
Nuclear proliferation is sweeping the globe, and the nuclear club is no longer exclusive. Even countries that have not acceded to the non-proliferation treaty-Brazil, Argentina, Egypt, Israel, Spain-are on the point of obtaining giant reactors. The more nuclear powers there are, the less control there will be and the greater the likelihood that the atom will be used in violence. That is what has led the authoritative Stockholm International Peace Research Institute to issue a gloomy prediction. Within nine years, 35 countries will be able to make atomic weapons. The future is very gloomy indeed.
Despite the growing danger, two years of SALT negotiations produced no positive results and the long-awaited world disarmament conference is no nearer reality. Yet we cannot give up on disarmament. I think the time is right for Canada to push hard for a special session of the UN general assembly devoted to disarmament.
If a world disarmament conference is still an impossibility, then a special session of the UN is the next best thing, for a special session would put a world spotlight on disarmament and mobilize public opinion on the necessity of disarmament. It would stimulate international action to make disarmament more likely, especially the creation of better world security, including permanent UN peacekeeping machinery, and develop a comprehensive program on disarmament, reaffirming the goal of general and complete disarmament. If such a special session were successful, it could serve as a stimulus for convening a world disarmament conference.
Disarmament can only be achieved if confidence is increased among nations. The non-aligned and the smaller countries have an increasingly important role to play in building a spirit of international confidence. This task is directly connected to development, since there can be no confidence in a world situation in which 30 per cent of the world's population receives and controls 70 per cent of the world's income.
What is at issue-as the UN has repeatedly made clear throughout this second development decade-is the continuing validity of the economic system which has dominated the world since the great economic expansion of the industrialized nations a century ago. We cannot have a stable and healthy world unless the enormous disparity between the affluent nations and those millions in Africa, Asia and Latin-America who suffer from poverty, malnutrition and lack of hope can be reduced and eventually eliminated.

Only this weekend the United Nations has again proven its value with the publication of a report, "The Future of the World Economy", which amasses a huge body of data to show that world resources will be sufficient to support a growing population and higher living standards without inevitable environmental damage. What is still needed is a reform of relations between developed and developing nations to share that economic growth. I will quote only one paragraph from this remarkable document to show that the mobilization of political will is our chief problem:
To ensure accelerated development, two general conditions are necessary: first, far-reaching internal changes of a social, political and institutional character in the developing countries and, second, significant changes in the world economic order.
The debate on the new international economic order has opened a new chapter in international relations, in which the sixth and seventh special sessions of the general assembly, along with the adoption of the charter of economic rights and duties of states, have so far been the key points.
I am often asked what the new economic order is all about. It is not a club or an association or some sort of economic miracle. It is, rather, a process to provide rapid economic and social development in the developing countries which contain the majority of mankind. It is a determination to provide the basics of life-food, shelter, education, medicine and job opportunities for every human being. It is a plan to make nations self-reliant so that the people within them can find true human liberation in their own lives.
In short, the global reform proposed by the new international economic order embraces: eradication of mass poverty and unemployment; stable and equitable return for commodities; self-sufficiency in food; reform of rules governing international trade; and an increased share in industrial activities for developing countries. Further proposals include an increased flow of assistance on concessional terms based only on need and equity, and equitable sharing in the global economic decisionmaking process.
The response of Canada to this challenge has been splendid-in rhetorical terms. The speeches of the Prime Minister and the former external affairs minister have been impressive. So, too, is the government's one-year old strategy for international development cooperation, a 21-point, multidimensional policy which supports the main lines of the new economic order.
I unhesitatingly support this strategy because it begins the process of moving away from aid as the only expression of our humanitarian concern. The strategy makes a commitment to the reform of the international trade and monetary systems which are at the root of mass poverty. Canada's total policy includes increased aid to the least developed and a willingness to move forward on commodity agreements, trade liberalization and industrial co-operation. It is weak on specifics, but the direction of the policy is accurate.
October 18, 1976

The principal problem with the strategy, as I discovered in a tour of the country, is that few Canadians have ever heard of it. The government, preoccupied with the domestic economy, has not promoted it. The media have all but ignored it. The result is that Canadian public opinion lags far behind the reality of the interlocking nature of global problems highlighted by the special UN conferences on population, food and human settlements. For its part, parliament, in its usual inversion of priorities, devotes very little attention to international development.
There is, in short, scarcely any pressure on the government to implement its own strategy. The pressure is the other way- not to allow more imports from "cheap labour" countries; not to share the mineral resources on the continental shelf beyond the 200-mile economic zone; not to pay any more than we have to for third world commodities.
Our direct foreign aid, as a percentage of GNP, has been cut-the ironic victim of domestic restraint. Our bilateral aid is still heavily tied to Canadian business. Our role in the important negotiations at the fourth United Nations trade and development conference was marked by resistance to the third world rather than support.
What the government has signalled to the UN in the first year of this new policy is timidity and drift rather than the innovative action so desperately needed. What the government has signalled to Canada in the throne speech is that international affairs are not very important. I call on the new Secretary of State for External Affairs to involve Canada more deeply in the work of the UN. He is a practical man and undoubtedly wants specific suggestions. Here are some. First, reconstitute the subcommittee on international development which during the last session did such valuable work in opening up ways in which Canada can help bring about trade and monetary reform. Second, increase the share of CIDA's budget going to non-governmental organizations which are the only effective public education instrument we have. Boost the mere $35,000 the government provides the United Nations Association of Canada so that it can do the information job it is capable of. Third, involve more Canadians in international development by enabling CIDA to honour its matching fund program which currently is restricted to matching only 54 cents for every dollar raised privately. Fourth, demonstrate Canada's determination to reach .7 per cent of GNP in development assistance by raising our commitment at least as much as our defence budget which goes up by an inflation factor plus 12 per cent a year. Last, press for the creation of a minister of state for international development who would be able to give full time to the necessary watchdog function of CIDA and also raise the level of public participation in Canada's role internationally.
The demands of a new order and their implications for our way of life must enter the daily consciousness of Canadians. This is a job for more than government, but if government does not take the lead in helping Canadians understand what the United Nations is calling for, there is faint prospect that the changes required will be supported by the voters.
The Address-Mr. Cyr
With the arousal of political will there is every reason to hope for a better future. The technology to make it possible is exciting. Recently, I visited the Wheat and Maize Improvement Centre in Mexico, one of the principal agricultural research centres in the world and home of the green revolution. Funded partly by Canada, the centre's work in developing new strains of maize, wheat, barley, sorghum and triticale has dramatically raised world cereal yields in the past decade with the prospect of greater gains ahead as the technology is applied.
The experts I talked with are agreed that the world has the capacity to feed billions more people than are now living. It is a strange world where the scientists give reasons for hope and the politicians despair. Perhaps we should all step back a pace and survey the wide scene as Barbara Ward did at the conclusion of "The Home of Man", written for Habitat:
In this time of reassessment, in this age of questioning as intense as any since the great debates of the millenium before the birth of Christ, there is promise of an extraordinary and almost wholly unforeseen fusion of ideas which, separated and even hostile for many centuries, now seem capable of that mutual interpenetration which, in the nuclear as in the intellectual world, can release floods of new energy, new directions, new possibilities, new beings, new forms.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to congratulate you and wish you great success in the office you have held in the House over the past year. The Sudbury constituents are proud of their elected representative, and we were able to appreciate your many talents during the first session of this Parliament. I wish also to congratulate the movers of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne for their excellent presentations.
In October 1974, I did not have the opportunity to take part in the Speech from the Throne debate, and I want to tell the House how proud I am to represent the Gaspe constituency in the Canadian Parliament. The people in the Gaspe constituency have given their vote to the Liberal party because they know that Liberal governments have always demonstrated their concern for economically poorer regions, and the development we have witnessed these past few years is surely evidence of this. My duty, ever since I have been their elected representative, has been to make sure that they are well provided for.
In the 1974 election, Gaspe was the only riding with two candidates only, one Liberal and one Conservative. In my opinion, this is an historical fact which must be brought before the House.
I am glad that the Speech from the Throne deals with the equality of opportunity for all Canadians. I would like to read again this excerpt which is very important for the regional development. I quote;
While it is essential to national unity that all Canadians believe we have an equal opportunity to be fully ourselves in a cultural sense, it is just as essential to unity that we enjoy equal opportunities for individual and regional economic fulfilment.
166

The Address-Mr. Cyr
To translate Canada's economic potential into real growth and equality of opportunity, we must be both clear-sighted in our recognition of the obstacles which lie in our path, and united in our determination to remove them.
On the economic level, the Gaspe peninsula which I represent benefitted from special agreements for the social and economic development of eastern Quebec. Signed in 1968, this general agreement for Canada-Quebec cooperation gave results which in some cases go beyond the estimated objectives.
The agreement contributed to the implementation of infrastructures which are very important for the development of the area. It is now a matter of launching programs to stimulate the establishment of productive occupations and consolidate jobs in traditional sectors. Negotiations are under way between both levels of government and the people in eastern Quebec, particularly Gaspe, request the signature of another special agreement or of auxiliary agreements to set up sectorial programs for the economic development of the area while maintaining the objective of job creation.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) must pay particular attention to the allocation of budgets for the coming years to favour economically deprived areas. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) must have at his disposal the necessary funds to meet his obligations with the provinces for the development of slow growth areas in Canada.
The government must not apply their budgetary restrictions in areas with low income or very high unemployment. I venture to suggest to the ministers, particularly to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), that air and road communications in Gaspe leave much to be desired and that there is room for some improvements. It is inconceivable that in 1976 Gaspe cannot yet boast a 6,000-foot runway nor the proper flight control facilities.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks on the fishing industry in eastern Canada and more particularly in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. I take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. LeBlanc) on his recent appointment as Minister of Fisheries and the Envionment and wish him the same success he had as Minister of State responsible for Fisheries and acting Minister of the Environment.
In the last few years, it has become increasingly obvious that the intensive fishing practised by foreign fleets off the Canadian coast, in particular that of ground fish on the eastern coast, would lead to a disastrous situation. The fish population, formerly abundant, have reached dangerously low levels. The very existence of the Canadian communities that depend on fishing for their livelihood is therefore threatened. The Liberal government, under the leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), signed bilateral agreements with several countries which had access to our fishing areas thereby allowing Canada to extend from 12 to 200 miles off-shore its territorial sovereignity with regard to fishing. That decision is most important for the future of that industry in Canada. All members and all Canadians congratulate the ministers and their officials who participated in the drafting and the signa-
[Mr. Cyr.l
ture of the agreements between countries. In fact, Mr. Speaker, those agreements are being used as models by those countries which are now facing a similar situation. In extending the fishing zone to 200 miles, the government has shown a genuine interest in fishing industries in Canada.
Since 1974, the government has spent more than $130 million to support fishing industries and more specifically those on the east coast. The Department of Environment has a price support program for fishermen and for companies processing first quality ground fish. In addition, the government of Quebec also has several programs for fishing industries and a recent agreement has been concluded between the provincial government and processing plant owners under which employees are guaranteed a standard working week. With decreasing catches in the gulf, some plants can only give a few days of work to their employees every week. With the new Quebec program employees can look forward to a normal income every week. However we hope that all those programs will be temporary and that conditions will be normalized in a near future, let us hope before 1980.
Although the governments have implemented satisfactory programs to assist fisheries, prospects are not very encouraging because stocks of red fish and cod in several areas of the gulf have been seriously depleted, so that the quotas for those two species will be considerably reduced for 1977. In order to replenish those stocks, it is essential to restrict fishing in the immediate future lest the survival of fisheries be jeopardized in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Quebec fishermen will experience a difficult period as long as the stocks are not restored, because large trawlers operating in the gulf will have to fish elsewhere, more specially on the Atlantic coast. The government has given financial support to fishermen whose home port is in the gulf to compensate for the longer trips they will have to make as well as the problems faced by those who fish in unknown areas.
Since September 28, cod fishing in the Gaspe area and the north of New Brunswick is closed up to three miles from the coast. The quota of fish set by the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries (ICNAF) in area T4 has been exceeded. If we have reached the aim at the end of September, it is due to the exceptional quantities of cod taken earlier this year by trawlers from Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, more particularly in January, February and March. For the remaining of 1976 the minister has decreed that Newfoundland and Nova Scotia trawlers will no longer be allowed to catch redfish in the gulf and cod in the southern part of the gulf. That is not enough to preserve fish stocks in the gulf.
To share out equally the number of fish that can be landed in a season and to protect the fishing industry in Quebec and in northern New Brunswick, I recommend that the Gulf of St. Lawrence as a whole be reserved to fishermen whose home port is the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and that fishing for some species such as redfish and cod be prohibited in January,
October 18, 1976

February and March for the next two years. And I think that in the speech he made on October 14 the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) echoed my ideas, when he said, as reported in Hansard, page 64, I quote:
I also believe that in order to develop a sound management scheme for our fisheries, consideration should be given to such factors as the time of the year when fish can be most efficiently caught, and here the fishermen's knowledge should be utilized. Consideration should also be given to the seasonal variations in the quality of fish, as well as other biological factors relating to the spawning period. We cannot continue in our old ways and habits if we are serious in our intention to rebuild our fisheries resources, and this applies to all ships licensed to fish on our banks, whether they be Canadian or ships of other nations.
Mr. Speaker, I fully agree with that statement of the official spokesman for the opposition, when he says that the government should immediately take very drastic measures.
Lately, the government amended the unemployment insurance program for fishermen, and those changes should come into effect this fall. Fishermen will be able to draw their unemployment benefits during the first week of November instead of December, while the deadline remains the week of May 15. The main changes provide fishermen with supplementary benefits based on the regional rate of unemployment. Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the House that these changes to the Unemployment Insurance Commission Regulations will benefit mostly fishermen in the Gaspe Peninsula, !les-de-la-Madeleine and even those in northern New Brunswick; congratulations to the ministers who introduced these changes!
In the last few years, grants available for building fishing boats of 30 to 75 feet have declined; I therefore ask the government to take the necessary steps to continue this program of grants to the fishing boat building industry to allow a rational renewal of the fleet, not grants to build new fishing boats but to renew old ones.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and his government hold close to their heart the well-being of our people, particularly working families, the unemployed and non-organized people. He has demonstrated it in the Speech from the Throne and again in a special way in his speech to the House last Wednesday. This speech is well worth reading by all Canadians as it demonstrates that both the CLC president and the leader of the NDP are wrong to criticize the anti-inflation legislation without offering alternative solutions. The failure of the day of protest against the anti-inflation measures on October 14 is abundant proof that the Canadian people support their government in its fight against inflation.
The Prime Minister drew a very realistic picture of the impact the controls had over the Canadian economy. The workers from Gaspesia, whose income is one of the lowest in Canada, agree that the anti-inflation measures had positive effects on the area, the province and the whole of Canada.
My constituents are convinced that the anti-inflation controls are necessary and they already have contributed in reducing the inflation rate. Those who disapprove of this program are the leaders of large labour unions and the directors of big companies. This demonstrates the effectiveness of the program which benefits small wage-earners and hurts mostly those who want to taker over political power.
The Address-Mr. Cyr
Many financial institutions in Canada as well as businessmen regrouped within the Canadian boards of trade have urged both the federal and provincial governments to reduce their expenses, without ever indicating clearly where these budgetary cuts should be made. When we travel from one end of the country to the other, we realize that our larger centers- such as Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver-are those which contributes most inflation. When considering budgetary cuts, the government must therefore make sure that all departments pay special attention to the projects which have been postponed for several years in the regions which are economically weaker and where the unemployment rate is the highest.
The right hon. Prime Minister said on his recent visit in Riviere-du-Loup that he was opposed to budget cuts in low economic growth regions by cancelling social measures. In the Gaspe region we live in an area where people are already in a position in which they cannot even contribute to inflation.
Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to hear in the Speech from the Throne that the government is also contemplating measures to make it easier for small business to gain access to financial assistance and other services provided by various departments, the Federal Business Development Bank and financial institutions in the private sector. Small businesses, managed by their owners, are the main job providers in many of our towns and villages in Gaspe. The economic structure in the Gaspe peninsula is heavily relying on seasonal activities, like agriculture, forestry, fisheries, tourism and construction. In order to make a decent living, a great number of Gaspesians have to be jacks-of-all-trades.
1 therefore feel that those new assistance programs to small businesses are indeed very timely for the development of the Gaspe peninsula and all eastern Quebec. They tie in with the recommendations of the Gaspe Chamber of Commerce which states as follows in a brief dated May 1976, and I quote:
That the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, in cooperation with other departments, Gaspe businessmen and economic organizations of that area, set up a commission whose specific purpose would be to conduct research, to give initial impetus to the industrial and commercial development of that area of the province, and to achieve a just balance between the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors of our activities;
That more moneys in a future agreement between Quebec and Canada be assigned to the development of industry, and more particularly small businesses, with a view to making it more supple, more easily accessible, less prone to exporting profits and less susceptible to general stoppages which paralyze and check the economic activity of the whole community.
Despite numerous programs initiated by the federal government in the last few years to fight unemployment, rate of unemployment is still very high in that area. At a recent meeting of the Liberal party in Matane, the delegates proposed that the federal government implement a job creating program for several years and not only the winter months. I am proud of the new direct job creation program announced in the speech from the throne. It will be most beneficial to the Gaspe peninsula has a chronically high unemployment level.
This new job creation program should promote projects which are beneficial to the community. However, many organ-

izations and municipalities do not have the financial means to purchase the required building supplies and equipment to carry out projects which are necessary to the community. I thus suggest that other federal departments cooperate with the Department of Manpower and Immigration and contribute to the financing of a portion of the building supplies required to carry out some projects. We hope that some departments will make additional contributions for the development of marinas and wharfs for traditional fishing, for the construction of breakers along our coasts, and for a number of other projects which could easily fall under the direct job creation program.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word about unemployment insurance. Indeed it is mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. I think it is very disappointing that some beneficiaries can hardly have their problems solved. There is certainly lack of communication between the commission staff and beneficiaries. I am sure that the staff is looking forward to help but the problem seems to be the amount of travelling claimants have to do to get information. It is unthinkable that some citizens of Gaspe have to travel 100 miles or more to settle an unemployment insurance problem. The commission will have to establish more extensive service in its unemployment insurance office on the north shore of Gaspe at Sainte-Anne-des-Monts. This is an urgent need for the constituency of Gaspe.
I should like to deal with another subject today, the parliamentary reform. We are aware that Parliament is the heart of democracy in Canada and that great progress has been made since 1968 toward concrete and positive changes to upgrade this institution which is imperfect and too close to tradition. Most hon. members want significant changes to make Parliament both more efficient and more modern and to give a new value to the role of parliamentarians. I am far from willing to sway from the principle according to which democracy must be safeguarded. But we can do it while accepting a careful planning of work for each session of Parliament, and the examination of bills can be made according to a fixed schedule, ensuring the good operation of a more rational and more efficient forum, while enabling a more humane and more intelligent participation by parliamentarians. Restricting the lenght of the speeches made by parliamentarians of all parties does not detract from the value of a debate. Very strict rules must be established in order take into account the fact that there are now four parties in this House.
Debates have become repetitive and stray more and more from the subject matter under consideration. We are here in Parliament to decide the fate of Canadians and we are wasting valuable time on debates which go on for months when they could be completed in a few days. The opposition must be granted the rights and the means to put their views forward in a thorough but not dilatory manner, thus eliminating every possibility of repeating the same elements of debate at the various stages of the legislative process. Debates must be restricted to the subject matter under consideration and the quality of speeches must be upgraded.

In a speech he delivered yesterday in Quebec City, the Leader of Her Majesty's Opposition said the following, and I quote from Le Devoir of October 18:
Quebec City (by Lise Bissonnette)-It is quite clear, and Mr. Joe Clark said it in French in Quebec City: His party "will continue to refrain from proposing immediate or detailed solutions" to the present economic and language problems, regardless of all pressures.
First, there is a "political reason" for this, he said; "the solutions of the fall of 1976 are not going to determine the results of the 1978 general election".
If the opposition leader tells the Canadian people outside the House that he will not put forward any solutions to the present economic and language problems, then why hold debates in the House of Commons if the opposition is only trying to criticize instead of proposing solutions? I infer from that statement that a Progressive Conservative may be defined as an economist who knows all the answers to the events of the past year.
Mr. Speaker, it is urgent to amend the procedures of the House, and particularly to find an updated voting system. It is ridiculous for parliamentarians to have to be called by a bell which sometimes rings from two to three hours before the vote is taken. What a waste of time and money for Canadians! Moreover, the whole staff of the House must wait for the vote to be over before moving on to other work. If this is what we call a productive system, Canada is in a sad way. The members of the Liberal causus have made representations to the committee responsible for studying the procedures of the House. We are in favour of negotiating the changes suggested by the official opposition. However, if it is impossible to reach a consensus, the federal government will have to act since the interests of Canadians are at stake.
In closing, I should like to congratulate in my own name and on behalf of my fellow citizens all my colleagues who have been chosen to perform very important duties within the cabinet. I should like to assure them of my full cooperation. To the hon. member for London West (Mr. Buchanan), Minister of Public Works, I wish much success in his new duties. He has already done very well early in his mandate by visiting several communities in eastern Quebec and northern New Brunswick. The efforts made by the minister to learn French since he came to Ottawa, that is since 1968, are worth mentioning in the House and should be held as an example before the other members. If all Canadians showed the same good will as the Minister of Public Works, we would not have any linguistic and cultural problems in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to add some remarks to those made by my colleagues in this debate. It has been said by several speakers in this debate that the throne speech was a rather sterile document, that in fact it did not indicate any real grasp by the government of the problems that we are facing. The

gaps in the address, the obvious omissions, were apparent to all, I think. As one commentator 1 heard on the day of delivery of the throne speech said, it was blander than usual. That is as kind as one can be.
Rather than deal with the language and cultural problems, as the government did extensively in the throne speech, we should have heard what will be done about the high interest rates that are being paid by Canadians. No mention was made of how we will deal with the serious balance of payments problems or how we will go about reducing them into more manageable levels. There was'some mention of productivity.
We are told in the throne speech that there will be more boards, more words, more discussions, more dialogue, more advertising and more slogans. But let us get right to the point. I do not believe that Canadian workers, per se, are less productive than workers in any other country. This has never been proven. I think our workers, given the equivalent in facilities and tools, are just as productive as workers in any other country in the world. I question the scale used to determine productivity, the methods, the formula or the process of weighing one economy against another.
Look at the taxation provisions and at the government's attitude toward depreciation provisions for plant and machinery. Look at the interest rates which must be paid by industry to acquire new machinery. Examine fully and carefully the restrictions placed on corporate profits and dividends, coupled with the high interest rates, and you will see the root of the problem.
Talking about productivity will not solve the problem. The government, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) know the root cause of low productivity on the scales we are using in Canada. Representatives of labour and industry have stated their concerns for years. All their words fell on deaf ears.
We lack commitment to a strong secondary industrial base in this country. The former minister of industry, trade and commerce, who is now the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), told our standing committee that he did not feel Canada could develop a secondary industrial base. He later took the course which we see used by many ministers-that being more dialogue and more discussion-and finally he stated that he was going to take a sectoral approach and develop an industrial strategy based on sectors. I think he stated we may end up with 18 or 20 different industrial strategies. This is just another idea to get away from the main point at issue here. This minister and his successor, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) sat in their places and allowed-

speechtext:
Look at the 1974 election. The government said it would not introduce controls, yet it did so. We know all about the government's big lie technique. At any rate, this minister and the succeeding minister sat in their places and watched a provision put into the AIB legislation, through a regulation, which caused research and development to be grouped in the same grouping as advertising, sales promotion and donations to charity. While this provision has now been removed, it caused a pause in research, caused many projects to be stoped or slowed down and caused hundreds of industrial projects to be shelved.
In fact, when the people in industrial research called the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce inquiring about the AIB regulation, the people in the department were not aware that such a regulation had been put in place. We had one department imposing a regulation and another department not knowing anything about it. Perhaps the former minister would like to comment on that at some time because, as I recall, he was there at that time.
Today we hear much about technological advances in industry, yet we are looking at a working paper and proposed legislation to change the patent laws in Canada. If this legislation proceeds, it will have a disastrous effect on the development of advanced technology in Canada. It will make it difficult not only to import technology, but it will almost preclude Canadian inventors and innovators from the foreign market. If the proposed patent law is put in place, we will have

October 18, 1976
The Address-Mr. Kempling
no patent legislation in Canada in ten years' time because what it is suggesting is that we go along for a ten year period and at the end of that period reassess it. However, when we read the legislation we find that what the government really wants to do is eliminate patents altogether. If the proposed legislation is enacted, the only country in the world which will have similar patent provisions will be the Soviet Union.
We have heard comments from every quarter of the economy regarding cutbacks in research and development, and we have already seen an exodus of many research projects to countries which have more favourable economic climates and fewer restrictions. If we carry the bleak research prospects which now face Canadian industry and the proposed patent laws to a conclusion, the future is not at all encouraging. The people mainly responsible for putting together the proposed patent legislation are themselves deficient. As far as I can determine, none of them has any extensive knowledge of the practical or historical aspects of patents. They have decided they are going to change our patent laws, and without consultation with patent attorneys, patent agents or the Patent Institute they have written a new proposed patent act. I understand that they have even suggested they have a priority on this, which I find deplorable.
In concert with the winding down of research funding we find the Treasury Board has issued an instruction under the folio TB Circular No. 1976-2, and this document restricts government scientists from attending non-government sponsored scientific conferences. The circular states that only one person may attend. Earlier this month-from October 4 to October 8, to be exact-the Canadian Aeronautics and Space Institute held its tenth congress in Ottawa. Between 200 and 300 prominent scientists attended and more than 60 learned papers were presented. Even though the congress was held in Ottawa, only one government scientist was allowed to attend. I, personally, find this restrictive regulation deplorable. Anyone who thinks about it will realize that one scientist cannot possibly have the time nor the expertise for every aspect of aeronautics and space, and I hope the new Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner) will see fit to have this restriction lifted.
Let me turn for a few moments to the anti-inflation program. Our inflation has eased slightly this year, but let us put it in its proper perspective. Food and food prices are not inlcuded under the AIB legislation. The food cost figures which go into the consumer price index have dropped or have remained relatively stable. As we understand it, this is due to a drop in the price of imported products. However, if we remove food from the consumer price index and look at inflation in that light, we will find that our inflation rate is still 9.4 per cent, not the 6.5 per cent which the AIB is advertising. I think it is a fraud on the people of Canada for the AIB to take credit for a drop in food prices when in fact food does not come under their regulations. A drop in inflation from 12 per cent to
9.4	per cent is not as dramatic as a drop from 12 per cent to
6.5	per cent.

It is ironic that people in industry and in the scientific community can see many solutions to our economic problems, both national and international, but find they are restricted by government regulations and poorly thought-out policies or, in fact, no policies at all. At recent meetings of the OECD and the International Monetary Fund, and at the meeting called a few months ago by President Ford which was convened in Puerto Rico, the call was for stricter fiscal and monetary restraint. In fact, the IMF chairman at the conference recently held in Manila hinted strongly that unless some countries put in place monetary legislation or regulations to control the amount of money being printed, and unless they are prepared to help themselves, perhaps the IMF would restrict loans to those countries and not rush to their aid.
The same message was set forth in recent OECD releases and it was the theme of the conference held recently in Puerto Rico. In Canada, the printing of money in the past few years has been in the order of 12 per cent to 15 per cent annually and in the most recent period, if it has not been adjusted, it was 27 per cent on an annual basis. Because of high interest rates, serious distortions are occurring in our economy. The bank rate is at an all-time high and Canadian businessmen are being attracted to purchasing products outside Canada where interest rates are considerably lower. In fact, it is possible to finance inventory outside Canada at about half our rate.
The spin-off effect of this to the business community will be disastrous if it is allowed to continue for long. If a purchaser of manufactured goods can purchase them abroad at a price competitive to domestic production, and can finance his purchase at half our bank rate, why should he ever purchase in Canada? When you reflect upon the long term effects of this fact of business life, Mr. Speaker, you can see ahead a continuing trade deficit, a continuing balance of payments problem and a bleak future for any small and medium-sized Canadian manufacturer.
Clearly, interest rates must come down; we cannot allow them to continue at this high rate. I know of companies which can finance their inventory at fixed rates of exchange and fixed interest rates of 6 Vi per cent or 7 per cent offshore. They can take advantage of container shipping and bring goods in during the Seaway season for the best possible freight rate; but looked at in the long term, this spells disaster for many small and medium-sized manufacturers.
Many industries have reacted and are searching for ways to reduce operating costs. A company contacted me recently and laid before me a program they wanted to start but, because of Anti-Inflation Board regulations, they cannot. The program would increase productivity and stabilize prices and might, over a period of time, even reduce their prices. They wanted to install an incentive cost reduction program which would require the co-operation of all employees. It would not result in the loss of any jobs, but would increase productivity, improve efficiency and help keep the company competitive in the domestic market against imported competition. It was a simple

program. They targeted for a certain number of dollars a day by which to reduce operating costs. Multiplied by the number of working days in the year, it gave an annual reduction. They proposed to share a portion of the saving in the form of an incentive bonus to employees. A portion would, of course, accrue to the management. The portion that would accrue to the employees could earn some of them as much as $1,000 a year more than they presently receive.
The Anti-Inflation Board stepped in and said they could not allow it; that there was a collective bargaining agreement which brought them under the umbrella of the AIB. They were told they could not adopt this type of program because it would raise the earnings of employees above the set level. In spite of the fact that the proposal would increase the productivity of the firm, improve its efficiency and reduce overhead, they were not allowed to adopt it. That is a deplorable situation, Mr. Speaker, and it is one of the inequities of the AIB program. The portion that the company would have retained would have driven their profits above the 85 per cent level and so it caused them difficulties.
There are many subjects that we had expected would be covered in the Speech from the Throne. We were speculating on its contents before it was presented. Maybe I did not look at it thoroughly enough, but I thought, in view of the difficulties facing the country and the expected day of protest on October 14, as well as the problems expressed to me by people in every walk of life and the business community in particular, that it would be a gung ho document. I expected it would give the people some hope for an end to their problems.
Instead, we were treated to a very bland document, one that fell far short of what the government is capable of. I think they are capable of producing a better document than that, for 1 have a great deal of confidence in some of the people in the departments. I do not have much confidence in many of the ministers, but some of the people in the departments are very competent and I think are capable of producing a document to give the people hope that in the years ahead their problems would be solved and they would reach the standard of living they deserve.
We got a disappointing document. The only thing we can look forward to now is the budget speech. If it does not have more in it than the Speech from the Throne, then there are serious times and trouble ahead of us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his courtesy and understanding following a temporary absence of a few seconds. I appreciate it greatly.
First, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) and the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They did their job with dignity and once again showed how well they can represent their constituents here.
I should also like to join with all those who paid tribute to our late colleague, Mrs. Albanie Morin. As we all know, she quickly won the admiration of all members in this House, and her death saddens us deeply. To her family and relatives, I extend my deepest sympathy.
With regards to the Speech from the Throne, I welcome the obvious fact that in that speech the principles that have always been the strength of the Liberal party are not only safeguarded but reaffirmed, especially with respect to bilingualism in relation to national unity, the quest for a formal constitutional independance, the reinforcement of the structure of Canadian agriculture, the fight against regional inequalities, respect for the collective bargaining, while at the same time promoting cooperation rather than antagonism, the protection of small businesses and respect of the private sector, and placing a great deal of emphasis on the fact that a notion of social conscience must accompany that of profit.
But today I should like to deal with two specific topics mentioned in the Speech from the Throne and dealing with individual freedom; first, a human rights bill, and second, the broadcasting of the debates of this House. With respect to a human rights bill, the speech from the throne states, and I quote:
In a similar effort to remove obstacles to information and to equal opportunity, the Government will introduce a Human Rights Bill. The major effect of the Bill will be to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion, age, sex, marital status, or physical handicap. In particular, the Bill will establish the principle of equal compensation for work of equal value performed by persons of either sex. It will establish a citizen's statutory right to gain greater access to personal records in federal information banks and to correct that information when it is in error. It will also limit the gathering of personal information by the Government.
The Canadian Bill of Rights, for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, assented to on August 10, 1960, states, and I quote:
The Parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian Nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions; Affirming also that men and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law; And being desirous of enshrining these principles and the human rights and fundamental freedoms derived from them, in a Bill of Rights which shall reflect

October 18, 1976
The Address-Mr. Pinard
the respect of Parliament for its constitutional authority and which shall ensure the protection of these rights and freedoms in Canada:
Mr. Speaker, since December 10, 1948, the day of the adoption by the United Nations of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, there has been in many countries an increasing awareness of the necessity to legislate and create internal mechanisms to fight discrimination against individuals. In his speech for the Nobel prize presentation, Alexander Soljenitsyn said, and this is from a quotation previously made in this House:
A quarter of a century ago the creation of the United Nations raised great expectations for humanity. Alas, in an immoral world they also became immoral. These are not united nations but united governments where those who were really elected, those who imposed themselves by force and those who came to power through an armed takeover are all on the same footing. Because of the mercenary prejudices of the majority, the United Nations jealously watch over the freedom of some nations while they do not care for that of others. By an unofficial vote they refused to consider individual claims, the pleas of the individual, of ordinary people not important enough for that gigantic organization. The United Nations never tried to impose on governments, as a condition for admissibility, the Bill of Rights, the most significant document of its 25 years of existence, leaving the population at the mercy of governments they did not choose.
All Canadian provinces have enacted statutes respecting human rights in relation to discriminatory practices. Every provincial statute, except that of Prince Edward Island, contains provisions for the establishment of a human rights commission or, for Newfoundland, the appointment of a commissioner. The provinces have taken the lead in this field because discriminatory practices have tended to be more prevalent in matters under provincial jurisdiction in the areas of employment, accommodation and services and because so many more Canadians are involved in matters under provincial jurisdiction.
Existing anti-discrimination provisions of federal statutes and regulations are fragmentary. For example, part I of the Canada Labour Code, which deals with fair employment practices, applies to employment by organizations such as banks, railways, etc., under the jurisdiction of parliament but does not include employment by the Crown in right of Canada. There is no over-all body of law at the federal level to which persons may resort when they consider themselves to have been harmed by the iscriminatory practices of organizations or persons whose activities fall within the legislative authority of parliament. As well, there is no legislation providing for the establishment of standards on the basis of which personal information in government records is accurate, accessible to the individual and used only for authorized purposes.

On July 21, 1975, the Minister of Justice introduced in the House of Commons Bill C-72 entitled the Canadian Human Rights Act. In announcing the legislation, the minister said and I quote:
I believe that the government has put forth a comprehensive legislative measure for the protection of human rights and interests in Canada. This is a bill which should please all Canadians.
Devised to extend the Canadian Bill of Rights, this legislation has two main purposes:
1.	-To prohibit discrimination in all matters within federal government jurisdiction on the grounds of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status or conviction for an offence for which a pardon has been granted;
2.	-To establish measures through which the right to individual privacy can be better protected consistent with public order and well-being.
The bill provides for the establishment of a Canadian Human Rights Commission as a vehicle for investigating and preventing discriminatory practices in areas under federal jurisdiction.

The commission would also develop information and research programs to foster public understanding of human rights and freedoms in Canada.
Finally, Bill C-72 authorizes the government to establish a series of guidelines providing that any File it possesses and which contains personal information about the nature, reputation, financial situation, health, living conditions and way of life of an individual be exact, put away in a safe place, open to the person concerned and used by others only with an authorization.
Mr. Speaker, on December 11 and 12, 1975, during a federal-provincial conference on the rights of man, Canada made an important step towards the ratification of three documents of the United Nations concerning the rights of man: a covenant on economic, social and cultural rights, a covenant on civil and political rights and the optional protocol accompanying it, all of them having been adopted by the United Nations in 1966; thus, the goals of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights became written down in international legal documents. It is fortunate that some paragraphs of the Throne Speech let us hope that legislation in this field will be introduced in the cause of this session.
As for broadcasting the debates of the House, the Speech from the Throne declares on page 4:
The Government and all Parliamentarians are concerned about the extent to which the average citizen is informed about Parliament. The Government wishes to provide access to the Parliamentary process for as many Canadians as possible. It will therefore seek approval to enable the proceedings of the House of Commons to be broadcast.
Mr. Speaker, to my mind, this suggestion justifies more than ever the necessity for important changes in the Standing Orders, 1 mean far-reaching reforms.
As most of my colleagues and particularly the preceding speaker, the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr), and the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who spoke on that subject Friday afternoon, I know that Parliament is the heart of Canadian democracy and that since 1968 serious efforts which brought concrete and positive changes have contributed to improve that imperfect institution and, as the hon. member for Gaspe said, an institution which sticks too much to tradition. It is really to be hoped, Mr. Speaker, that another important phase will be covered to modernize the House of Commons and make it more efficient and also to enhance the role of parliamentarians.
I do not intend to make an exhaustive or academic study of the activities of Parliament. Indeed since 1968, the members can increasingly take part in the drafting of legislation; as an example, between October 8, 1970 and February 16, 1972- because statistics are available-21 committees of the House of Commons were set up and held 900 sittings. They called 2,751 witnesses and the record of their interventions make up over 30,000 pages.
I proceed from the ideal principal that a careful planning of the proceedings of each parliamentary session and the passage of bills according to a determined agenda ensure a more rational and efficient tribune while making the role played by
October 18, 1976

parliamentarians more humane and intelligent. I do not forget on the other hand that it is surely necessary to recognize to the opposition the right and the means to make its views known thoroughly but not in a dilatory manner and 1 would like to suggest substantial technical amendments which are however a safeguard for democracy.
The main grievances 1 have with respect to the Standing Orders of the House of Commons are as follows: First, unwarranted repetition of the same elements of discussion. Second, more often than not debates are impressed with partisan spirit rather than valuable or constructive criticism, hence we have far too many digressions in speeches. Third, we make improper use of the time and means put at the disposal of the opposition in the course of the various stages of consideration of bills in an attempt-often admitted-to prevent or unduly delay passage by a majority government; that is called "filibuster". Fourth, I find there is the highly abusive restraint of continual and too often useless physical presence in the House of Commons, making it impossible for the member to plan soundly and carry out effectively the diversified tasks which he or she could or should undertake. Fifth, a disorderly and overly exhaustive schedule of parliamentary business deprives the member from an essential and valuable presence in his riding and with his family. I submit that the implementation of the following principles is necessary if we mean to have a workable reform.
The first principle is that we must in fact
(a)	recognize that tbe opposition is entitled to have the right and means to make its views known, in a thorough and immediate manner, by eliminating the opportunity to reiterate the same arguments at the different stages of the procedure, bringing back the discussion to relevant points and thusly improving the quality of the debate.
The second principle which, in my view, is valid is the following:
(b)	: Carefully plan the member's presence in the House of Commons to make a more effective schedule possible.
Lastly, the third principle that we should adopt if we wish to make sensible improvements is as follows:
(c)	Establish a well ordained parliamentary schedule which would permit hon. members to carry out their political duties away from Parliament Hill and live a more normal family life.
Mr. Speaker, as a suggestion for the administration of these guidelines, I propose that the House adopt the following changes which are not restrictive in any way.
First of all, concerning the business hours of the House of Commons: in my humble opinion, the House should sit every day, except Monday or Friday, from 2 to 6 p.m., and then again from 8 to 10 p.m. This echoes the suggestion the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) made in the House last Friday to limit the number of working days in the House to four. Once again, and 1 do not wish to repeat what I have said, I want to practise what I preach, follow the guidelines and meet the grievances I indicated previously.
The Address-Mr. Pinard
As to the vote, when possible I think it should be deferred to a fixed date and to a determined time, except for urgent matters. Speeches should be limited to 15 or 20 minutes for each speaker, except for the official spokesman or the first speaker of each party who would be allowed 30 minutes.
Concerning private members' hour, I propose that it be held every second Wednesday night, that is from eight to nine o'clock and from nine to ten o'clock, with the vote, if any, deferred to the day and date determined for that purpose. As to opposition days, they should be established according to a parliamentary schedule.
The debates relating to the Speech from the Throne and to the budget speech should be reduced to sittings of six days for the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne and five days for the budget speech.
Most important of all is the parliamentary schedule. Each session should end June 23 at the latest, the eve of Saint John the Baptist's Day, the day of French Canada, until the day following Labour Day, that is at the beginning of September.
Having regard to debates on government bills, I propose a standing committee of parliamentary leaders to determine a time schedule for the House and the committees with power being granted to the government to impose its decision whenever an agreement is impossible. Recourse to this closure rule should be debatable by only one speaker for each party with a 30-minute time limit in each case.
In addition, we should limit to 10 minutes the speech delivered by the mover of an amendment put a second time at the report stage and to 10 minutes the speech of the governments's speaker.
Mr. Speaker, failure to raise quorum should bring the adjournment of the House only after the bells have rung for ten minutes to call members.
I think it is absolutely ridiculous, as I noticed it happened once last year, that because there is one member missing in the House to have the quorum, the House should lose precious hours and adjourn until the next day to resume its business. 1 hope this unfortunate experience will not occur again. It is not the fault of one party in particular, but I think that a minor change in the Standing Orders would prevent a new occurrence of a ridiculous and obsolete situation. Upon noticing that there is no quorum, we should ring the bells for ten minutes to call the members. As for the question period, I suggest that government members should have the same privileges as those extended to opposition members.
Finally, I will say a word about the committee of the whole. The votes on the consideration of each clause should be deferred and held at the same time. On various matters, I agree that the Speaker should be severe and not hesitate to intervene when the discussion departs from the subject under consideration. I agree with the suggestions that a special committee be set up for second reading of all bills that are acceptable to all parties, and also that the order paper should be simplified and made easier to understand. As for the

October 18, 1976
The Address-Mr. Brisco
standing committees, their membership should be limited to a maximum of 20 and quorum reduced to seven.
Several changes, Mr. Speaker, were discussed by the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, committee of which I am a member and on which I sat for five days during the summer break before Parliament came back last Tuesday. Because there is pressing need for those changes, committee members agreed to submit them for discussion to their respective caucuses in the next few days. Those changes are not necessarily all included in those I have just mentioned, but several of them, which were discussed and met with the general approval of the committee, are among those I have just talked about. I believe circumstances will justify those changes and if they are well explained to Canadians the latter, in all logic, will see that they are in their interest and that they will in no way affect true democracy.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, that parliamentary reform is urgent, fundamental and necessary. We will soon know where we stand with regard to the attitude of the various political parties towards the negotiated changes. I trust petty politics will be set aside to achieve a procedure truly worthy of a Parliament at once modern, humane, efficient as well as interesting, because I have just included all speeches on parliamentary reform in my argument on televising our debates. It is important that our Parliament should also become interesting. Concerned about offering the Canadian public both objective information of the business of Parliament and reports interesting and worthy of responsible public men, I feel that this parliamentry reform would justify televising the debates of this House, as suggested in the Speech from the Throne.

I hear a comment from across the chamber to the effect that it was too narrow a speech. The only thing that is narrow is the vision of the hon. member who made that remark. As a relatively new member from British Columbia, I have reviewed the Speech from the Throne with some care. I must say that in an area of concern to many Canadians it caused me a great deal of agony and some soul-searching. I
[Mr. Pinard.l
feel I am obliged to comment on one of the first points made in that speech:
Since 1968 the policy of official languages, supported by all parties represented in parliament, has been based on the principle of equality and on the right of Canadians to speak English or French according to their own will. An essential consequence, agreed by parliament, is that the federal government provide services in the two official languages in the national capital and wherever else there is sufficient demand for such services.
I call attention to the use of the word "policy" in that statement. Mr. Speaker, that policy is not supported by this member. In fact, it is not supported by a large number of members who sit in this House. It is not the policy which we support; it is, rather, the principle. We have no difficulty living with the principle, but when we see a policy of the nature we have seen so far we cannot but recognize that it is divisive and the subject of bitter debate across Canada. How can I associate myself with that type of federal bungling? When I sit in caucus and listen to the comments of our Francophone members and compatriots, one of my greatest embarrassments is that I cannot understand what they say.
